labs.interpret: Your lecture treats metals and mould together — they are detoxed simultaneously.

labs.name: PHQ-9
labs.why: Screening for depression and tracking severity over time.
labs.interpret: 5–9 mild, 10–14 moderate, 15–19 moderately severe, 20–27 severe. Item 9 asks about self-harm — never skip it.

labs.name: GAD-7
labs.why: Screening for generalised anxiety; also useful in panic, social anxiety and PTSD.
labs.interpret: 5–9 mild, 10–14 moderate, 15+ severe. A score of 10 or more is the recommended cutoff for further evaluation.

labs.name: Mood Disorder Questionnaire (MDQ)
labs.why: Screening for bipolar disorder — essential before starting an antidepressant.
labs.interpret: 13 questions on symptoms and function. A positive screen means a full evaluation, not a diagnosis.

labs.name: Urine toxicology
labs.why: Part of the medical workup that rules out substance-related causes of psychiatric presentation.
labs.interpret: Ordered alongside CBC, TSH and electrolytes before attributing symptoms to a primary psychiatric cause.

labs.name: Cognitive screening (MMSE / MoCA)
labs.why: Memory complaints and suspected cognitive decline.
labs.interpret: MoCA is more sensitive to mild impairment; correct for education.

labs.name: AUDIT-C and substance screening
labs.why: Alcohol and substance use as a driver of mood, sleep, liver and cardiac findings.
labs.interpret: Brief and well validated; ask everyone.

labs.name: Home blood pressure monitoring
labs.why: Confirming hypertension before treating, and excluding white-coat effect.
labs.interpret: A validated upper-arm device, twice daily for a week, is worth more than a single clinic reading.

labs.name: Orthostatic vitals
labs.why: Dizziness, syncope, fatigue and suspected dysautonomia.
labs.interpret: A fall of 20 systolic or 10 diastolic on standing defines orthostatic hypotension.

labs.name: Forced expiratory time
labs.why: A bedside screen for airflow obstruction, timed at the trachea.
labs.interpret: Your respiratory chart sets normal under 5 seconds; most texts call 6 seconds or more a positive test.

labs.name: Pulse oximetry
labs.why: Every respiratory presentation.
labs.interpret: 92% or less indicates a need for more advanced care; 88% or less means the emergency department.

labs.name: COPD Assessment Test (CAT)
labs.why: Symptom burden in COPD, used with exacerbation history to place the patient in a treatment group.
labs.interpret: A score of 33 is very severe and warrants specialist referral.

labs.name: Mould exposure questionnaire
labs.why: Structured intake and documentation where mould illness is suspected.
labs.interpret: Dr Jill Crista's questionnaire is the one your lecture recommends for documentation and intake.

Acne.note: Persistent adult acne with irregular cycles and hirsutism should be worked up as PCOS rather than treated as skin alone.

Allergic rhinitis.note: Intranasal corticosteroid outperforms an oral antihistamine for persistent symptoms; saline rinsing is the highest-yield non-drug measure.

Amenorrhea.note: Exclude pregnancy first, then separate hypothalamic (low energy availability, over-exercise) from PCOS and from prolactinoma.

Anemia, iron deficiency.note: Iron deficiency in an adult is a symptom, not a diagnosis — find the bleeding source. In men and post-menopausal women that means investigating the gut.

Anxiety.note: Panic before meals points at blood glucose rather than at anxiety. Screen with the MDQ before any antidepressant — an unrecognised bipolar patient can be flipped into mania.

Asthma.note: An inhaled corticosteroid belongs to every patient with persistent asthma; a LABA is never given alone. In an acute attack, wheeze that quietens is the airway closing, not improving.

Atherosclerosis.note: Cholesterol that will not shift with diet and lifestyle may have an environmental toxicant component — one of the flags from your mould lecture.

Autoimmune conditions.note: Always consider mould and toxicant burden in autoimmunity that resists treatment; screen for latent TB and hepatitis B before any biologic.

Back pain.note: Image only for red flags: saddle anaesthesia, bladder or bowel change and bilateral weakness mean cauda equina and an emergency MRI; fever, night pain and weight loss mean infection or malignancy.

Benign prostatic hyperplasia.note: A 5-alpha reductase inhibitor halves the PSA — double the measured value when interpreting. A hard or nodular prostate on the rectal exam changes the question entirely.

Bloating and gas.note: Your Mayan abdominal massage coursework names gastrointestinal and pelvic pain among its indications; it is a reasonable adjunct once obstruction and mass are excluded.

Bronchitis.note: Acute bronchitis is a clinical diagnosis — no test confirms it, and antibiotics belong only where you genuinely suspect bacterial infection or co-infection.

Candidiasis.note: Treatment-resistant candida is one of the presentations your mould lecture says should always prompt a mycotoxin workup; the OAT arabinose marker links the two.

Chronic fatigue syndrome.note: Pace rather than push — graded exercise can worsen post-exertional malaise. Brain fog with chronic fatigue and multiple systems involved is the pattern your mould lecture asks you to test for.

Chronic kidney disease.note: Review every drug and supplement for renal dosing. NSAIDs, high-dose vitamin C and many botanicals need reconsidering.

Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.note: Spirometry alone confirms the diagnosis — imaging is not needed for it. NAC is the most effective agent for mucus. Cessation is the only intervention that changes the trajectory; screen mood before varenicline.

Chronic pain.note: High urinary oxalates from fungal colonisation can mimic fibromyalgia and diffuse pain — worth remembering before settling on a central sensitisation label.

Cognitive decline.note: Exclude the reversible causes first — B12, thyroid, medication burden, alcohol, sleep apnoea and depression. New brain fog with other systems involved should raise mould.

Common cold.note: Test for a specific pathogen as soon as a patient in a high-risk group becomes symptomatic. In anyone under 19 on long-term aspirin or salicylates, a viral URI raises the risk of Reye's syndrome.

Congestive heart failure.note: Left-sided heart failure is the classic cause of a transudative pleural effusion. Daily weights catch decompensation before breathlessness does.

Conjunctivitis.note: Most cases are viral and self-limiting. A contact-lens wearer, photophobia, or vision change needs same-day ophthalmology.

Constipation.note: Correct constipation before any detox protocol — your mould lecture is explicit that toxins recirculate when the bowel is not moving.

Cough.note: The three commonest causes of chronic cough are upper airway cough syndrome, asthma and reflux. Cough beyond three weeks, or with haemoptysis, night sweats or weight loss, needs imaging and TB testing.

Depression.note: Five or more symptoms for at least two weeks, one of them depressed mood or anhedonia. Screen the MDQ before an antidepressant: SAMe, St John's wort and rhodiola can all trigger mania in a bipolar patient.

Diabetes mellitus, type 2.note: Check B12 in anyone on metformin for more than a few years. Berberine's glucose-lowering rivals metformin in trials but it inhibits CYP3A4 — review the whole medication list.

Diarrhea.note: Do not slow the gut where there is fever or blood in the stool — loperamide prolongs invasive infection.

Dysmenorrhea.note: Your Mayan abdominal massage coursework names dysmenorrhoea first among its indications. Pain that escalates over years, or with dyspareunia and subfertility, points at endometriosis.

Dyspepsia.note: Alarm features — weight loss, dysphagia, anaemia, vomiting, or new onset over 50 — mean endoscopy before empirical acid suppression.

Eczema.note: Eczema in an infant is often the first sign of mould illness, per your lecture. Emollients and barrier care are the base every regimen is built on.

Edema.note: Separate bilateral (cardiac, renal, hepatic, drug) from unilateral (DVT, lymphatic, local) — a unilateral swollen, warm, tender calf is a DVT until excluded.

Endometriosis.note: Your Mayan abdominal massage coursework lists endometriosis among its indications. A fixed retroverted uterus with nodular uterosacral ligaments on bimanual exam is the classic finding.

Fatigue and low energy.note: Work through the common causes before the interesting ones: anaemia, thyroid, sleep apnoea, depression, medication and alcohol.

Fertility and preconception.note: Your massage coursework names infertility among the indications, and your mould lecture asks you to screen for environmental toxicants where IVF has failed repeatedly. Start the male partner's semen analysis early.

Fibromyalgia.note: High oxalates from fungal colonisation can mimic fibromyalgia — worth excluding before committing to the label.

Food intolerance.note: Exclude coeliac disease before removing gluten — the serology only works while gluten is still being eaten.

GERD.note: Raise the head of the bed and leave three hours between the last meal and lying down. Taper a long-term PPI rather than stopping it — rebound acid is real. Peppermint oil must be enteric-coated or it makes reflux worse.

Gallstones.note: Ultrasound is first-line. Inspiratory arrest on right subcostal palpation — Murphy's sign — with fever means acute cholecystitis and urgent referral.

Gastritis.note: Test and treat H. pylori. Betaine HCl is contraindicated while the mucosa is inflamed or while on a PPI or NSAID.

Gingivitis.note: Persistent or severe periodontal disease should prompt a diabetes screen — the relationship runs both ways.

Gout.note: Aspirate a first presentation where infection is possible — negatively birefringent crystals mean gout, a positive culture means septic arthritis. Urate can be normal during a flare.

Hemorrhoids.note: Never attribute rectal bleeding to haemorrhoids without examining — and over 50, or with weight loss or altered bowel habit, colonoscopy first.

Hepatitis.note: Establish the cause before treating — viral, autoimmune, metabolic, alcohol and drug-induced take entirely different paths. Review every supplement for hepatotoxicity.

Herpes simplex.note: Start antivirals within 72 hours of prodrome. Suppressive therapy is worth discussing where recurrences are frequent or a partner is uninfected.

Hypertension.note: Confirm with home readings before treating. Screen for sleep apnoea in resistant hypertension. Liquorice and NSAIDs both raise blood pressure — check the supplement list.

Hyperthyroidism.note: Any sore throat or fever on an antithyroid drug needs an urgent white cell count — agranulocytosis. Avoid ashwagandha, which raises thyroid hormones.

Hypothyroidism.note: Take levothyroxine fasted, four hours away from calcium, iron, magnesium and coffee. Correct iron and selenium — conversion depends on them. High-dose iodine can worsen Hashimoto's.

Influenza.note: Rapid onset of fatigue, fever, myalgia and headache without loss of taste or smell points to influenza over COVID-19. Antivirals work best within 48 hours.

Insomnia.note: CBT-I outperforms hypnotics and its gains last. Screen for sleep apnoea and restless legs before prescribing anything sedating — ferritin under 50 drives restless legs.

Interstitial cystitis.note: A culture-negative painful bladder. Identify dietary triggers — coffee, citrus, alcohol and artificial sweeteners are the usual four.

Irritable bowel syndrome.note: Your massage coursework names IBS among its indications. Calprotectin separates it from inflammatory bowel disease and can spare a colonoscopy. Treatment-resistant IBS is on your mould lecture's list of presentations to test.

Kidney stones.note: Fluid volume beats every other measure. High-dose vitamin C raises oxalate — reconsider it in stone formers. Thiazides lower urinary calcium.

Lactation support.note: Check every medication and botanical for lactation safety. Your mould lecture allows PectaSol and probiotics in pregnancy and stops all other detox agents.

Menopause.note: Vaginal oestrogen is minimally absorbed and can be used where systemic therapy is not appropriate. Any post-menopausal bleeding is endometrial carcinoma until excluded.

Migraine.note: Riboflavin at 400 mg and magnesium have the best supplement evidence, both over 2–3 months. Limit acute medication to under 10 days a month or medication-overuse headache follows.

Nausea and vomiting.note: Nausea with headache, confusion and hyponatraemia in a lung cancer patient is a paraneoplastic syndrome, not a gut problem.

Neck and shoulder pain.note: Midline spinous tenderness after trauma needs imaging before mobilisation. Arm pain reproduced by extension, rotation and axial loading is radicular.

Obesity.note: Obesity is the commonest risk factor for obstructive sleep apnoea — screen with STOP-BANG. Exclude hypothyroidism and check for fatty liver.

Osteoarthritis.note: Weight loss and strengthening outperform every supplement in knee osteoarthritis. Radiographic change tracks poorly with symptoms.

Osteoporosis.note: Correct vitamin D and calcium before starting an antiresorptive. Never stop denosumab without a follow-on agent — rebound vertebral fractures follow.

Otitis media.note: A bulging, immobile, erythematous tympanic membrane is the finding. Many cases resolve without antibiotics — delayed prescribing is reasonable in the well child.

Parasites, intestinal.note: Treat on a positive stool test, not on suspicion. Eosinophilia on the CBC differential supports a parasitic cause.

Pneumonia.note: A lobar infiltrate on chest X-ray is what makes the diagnosis definitive — not the white count, the sputum stain or the blood gas. GI symptoms with hyponatraemia and a water-system exposure means Legionella and a urinary antigen test.

Polycystic ovary syndrome.note: Myo-inositol in a 40:1 ratio with D-chiro-inositol has the best supplement evidence. Letrozole beats clomiphene for ovulation induction. Exclude thyroid disease, prolactinoma and late-onset CAH.

Premenstrual syndrome.note: Vitex needs three cycles to judge. Symptom charting across two cycles distinguishes PMS from a mood disorder that merely worsens premenstrually.

Prostatitis.note: Chronic bacterial prostatitis needs 4–6 weeks of a drug that penetrates the gland. A boggy, exquisitely tender prostate with fever is acute prostatitis — do not massage it.

Psoriasis.note: Screen for psoriatic arthritis and for metabolic syndrome — both travel with it. Methotrexate and biologics need pre-treatment TB and hepatitis screening.

Raynaud's phenomenon.note: Beta blockers worsen it. A positive ANA with digital ulceration suggests secondary Raynaud's from a connective tissue disease rather than primary.

Rheumatoid arthritis.note: Symmetric MCP and PIP synovitis with over an hour of morning stiffness. Early DMARD therapy changes the outcome — do not delay while trialling supplements alone.

Sinusitis.note: Saline irrigation is the highest-yield measure. Treatment-resistant sinusitis is where your mould lecture asks for a nasal swab with BOTH bacterial and fungal components — the fungal side is the one commonly missed.

Sore throat.note: Score before swabbing, and swab before prescribing. In anyone under 19 on long-term salicylates, a viral illness carries Reye's syndrome risk.

Urinary incontinence.note: Supervised pelvic floor physiotherapy is first-line for both stress and urgency types. New incontinence with saddle anaesthesia and leg weakness is cauda equina — an emergency.

Urinary tract infection.note: Nitrofurantoin does not reach the kidney — flank pain and fever mean pyelonephritis and a different agent. D-mannose is prevention, not treatment.

Varicose veins.note: Check the ankle-brachial index before compressing any limb where arterial disease is possible. Diosmin and hesperidin have the best oral evidence.

Vertigo.note: Separate peripheral from central: sudden vertigo with any new neurological sign, or an inability to walk, is a posterior circulation stroke until excluded.

Wound healing.note: A non-healing lower limb wound needs an ankle-brachial index and a glucose check before anything topical. Zinc and vitamin C are the two nutrients that most often limit healing.

Bipolar disorder.note: Bipolar I needs one manic episode of at least a week; bipolar II needs a hypomanic episode of at least four days plus a major depressive episode; cyclothymia is recurrent dysthymic and hypomanic episodes over two years. AVOID SAMe, St John's wort, rhodiola, ginseng and high-dose caffeine — each can trigger mania or cycling. Light therapy also needs care.

Post-traumatic stress disorder.note: Psychotherapy is first-line — CPT, prolonged exposure and EMDR. Benzodiazepines are NOT recommended: they interfere with the extinction learning therapy depends on and carry a high dependence risk. The HPA profile is raised CRH with a blunted ACTH response and low cortisol — a sensitised negative feedback loop.

Adjustment disorder.note: Emotional or behavioural symptoms within three months of an identifiable stressor, out of proportion to it, resolving within six months of the stressor ending. That timeline is what separates it from MDD.

Obstructive sleep apnea.note: STOP-BANG first — a clinically relevant score is what supports polysomnography, the gold standard. Severity comes from the Apnea-Hypopnea Index, not the questionnaire or neck circumference. Obesity is the commonest risk factor; lateral decubitus sleeping helps and supine worsens it. Vitamin D deficiency tracks with having the condition, and the worse the deficiency the worse the symptoms.

Central sleep apnea.note: Cheyne-Stokes breathing is the associated pattern. Management is better control of the causative chronic conditions plus positive airway pressure — not the airway surgery or jaw devices used in obstructive apnoea. Opioids, sedatives, alcohol and smoking are root causes; NSAIDs are not.

Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.note: Pirfenidone and nintedanib are the antifibrotics. Quercetin may help but is not antifibrotic in mechanism. Honeycombing on high-resolution CT is the characteristic finding.

Bronchiectasis.note: Tram-track and signet-ring signs on CT. Treatment is infection control, bronchodilation, inflammation suppression and — above all — daily airway clearance. Antifibrotic therapy has no place in it.

Sarcoidosis.note: Raised 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D without supplementation, hypercalciuria, mild anaemia and a reversed albumin/globulin ratio. Do NOT supplement vitamin D blindly here. Prostacyclin derivatives are not a treatment — no pulmonary vasodilator without a right heart catheterisation first.

Cystic fibrosis.note: Recurrent bronchitis with haemoptysis, chronic sinus disease, greasy floating stools and failure to thrive. Elevated sweat sodium, chloride or potassium on quantitative pilocarpine iontophoresis confirms it.

Pulmonary hypertension.note: Right heart catheterisation is the gold standard — echocardiography screens, it does not confirm. Cor pulmonale is the complication to fear. Exertional dyspnoea with syncope and enlarged pulmonary arteries on plain film is the picture.

Pulmonary embolism.note: D-dimer is the first step where clinical likelihood is LOW; CT angiography is what rules it out. Blood gases classically show low oxygen with low CO2 from hyperventilation. A pleural friction rub points specifically at pulmonary infarction.

Respiratory failure and ARDS.note: Type 1 is hypoxaemic, type 2 adds CO2 retention — non-invasive positive pressure ventilation suits type 2. ARDS under the Berlin criteria requires an insult within one week, and injures capillary endothelial and alveolar epithelial cells. Keep oxygen to the minimum effective concentration — 60–100% risks oxygen toxicity.

Pulmonary nodules and lung cancer.note: Irregular border, large size, ground-glass appearance and older age suggest malignancy; concentric calcification suggests benignity. Small cell and squamous arise centrally with symptoms; adenocarcinoma and large cell peripherally without. Radon is the commonest cause after smoking; adenocarcinoma is commonest in non-smokers; small cell is the most aggressive. Brain, bone and liver are the usual metastatic sites. Hyponatraemia in small cell is paraneoplastic SIADH.

Pleural disease.note: Increased fremitus separates early lobar pneumonia from effusion — sound travels better through consolidated lung than through fluid. Transudates come from left-sided heart failure; exudates from pneumonia, malignancy and embolism. The visceral pleura is insensitive; pleuritic pain comes from the parietal pleura via the intercostal nerves, and diaphragmatic involvement refers to neck and shoulder. Pneumothorax needs a chest tube; a retained haemothorax risks empyema and fibrothorax.

Tuberculosis.note: Chronic cough with haemoptysis, night sweats and travel to an endemic area. No single test is definitive on its own — culture confirms. Drug-resistant TB is not prevalent in the United States.

COVID-19.note: Resveratrol is the agent that addresses both the inflammation and the thrombus formation. Return to normal activities needs symptom improvement AND no fever for 24 hours — not a negative test.

Mold and mycotoxin illness.note: Multiple symptoms across multiple systems together is the clinical clue. Order of work: correct nutritional deficiencies (iron, B12, B9, iodine, vitamin D, copper, zinc, thyroid), then foundations of sleep, food and stress, then gut and toxicant detox together, then infectious disease last. Do NOT detox during ongoing exposure, active colonisation, severe constipation or extreme sensitivity, and avoid glutathione, liver sauce and NAD+ while exposure continues. Treat sinuses last. Always consider mould when treating Lyme, EBV, seizures, autism, treatment-resistant SIBO, MCAS, chronic candida, infertility and cancer.

Atrial fibrillation.note: An irregularly irregular pulse is the bedside finding. Check thyroid function and screen for sleep apnoea — both drive it. Anticoagulation is decided on stroke risk, not on symptoms.

Deep vein thrombosis.note: Unilateral calf swelling, warmth and tenderness. Duplex ultrasound is first-line. Do not start a fibrinolytic supplement alongside anticoagulation without supervision.

Abdominal aortic aneurysm.note: A widened, expansile pulsation over 3 cm. Blood pressure control and smoking cessation slow expansion; size and growth rate decide repair.

Statin-associated muscle symptoms.note: Check CK where pain is severe. Correct vitamin D and thyroid before abandoning the statin; CoQ10 replaces what the drug depletes. Never combine a statin with red yeast rice.

Inflammatory bowel disease.note: Your mould lecture's “fuzzy dresser” case is an IBD patient whose inflammatory markers only normalised once a mould-contaminated piece of furniture left the house — worth remembering in inflammation that resists treatment.

Sexually transmitted infection.note: Screen partners and re-test after treatment. The protocol splits its plan by organism — bacterial vaginosis and candidiasis, herpes simplex, and human papillomavirus.

Erectile dysfunction.note: Erectile dysfunction is often the first sign of endothelial disease — work it up as a cardiovascular risk marker, not only as a sexual complaint.

Attention deficit disorder.note: Check iron and ferritin — low iron worsens attention and restless sleep. New-onset ADHD is on your mould lecture's list of presentations to test for mycotoxins.

Seizure disorder.note: Sudden-onset seizures with no family history is the presentation your mould lecture's second case study describes — testing confirmed exposure and the child was weaned off medication after relocation and detox.

Multiple sclerosis.note: Vitamin D status is both a risk factor and a modifiable target. Heat sensitivity (Uhthoff's phenomenon) makes hot exercise environments a practical problem.

Parkinson's disease.note: Constipation and loss of smell often precede the motor signs by years. Protein timing matters where levodopa is used — large protein meals compete with its absorption.

Hepatic steatosis.note: Weight loss of 7–10% is the intervention with the strongest evidence. Exclude alcohol, viral hepatitis and drug causes before calling it metabolic.

Celiac disease.note: Serology only works while gluten is still being eaten — test before removing it. Strict lifelong gluten avoidance is the treatment; screen for the deficiencies malabsorption leaves behind.

Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth.note: Treatment-resistant SIBO is one of the presentations your mould lecture says should always prompt a mycotoxin workup. Address motility, not just the overgrowth, or it returns.

Warts.note: Most resolve spontaneously over months to years. Anogenital warts need STI screening and cervical screening where relevant.

Burns.note: Depth and total body surface area decide referral. Cool with running water, never ice, and never break blisters routinely.

studyNotes.title: Pediatric Dermatology — Final Exam Study Guide
studyNotes.blurb: Each condition follows the same shape: aetiology and epidemiology, clinical presentation, naturopathic treatment, homeopathy keynotes, then conventional treatment and red flags.

sections.part: Approach to Skin Evaluation in Children
sections.title: Clinical History
body: HPI focuses on the time course of the eruption and its relationship to other symptoms.
Review of systems clues:
GI symptoms → suggests IgA-associated vasculitis (HSP) or hemolytic-uremic syndrome
Joint symptoms → suggests IgA-associated vasculitis (HSP) or Lyme disease
Headache/neurologic symptoms → suggests meningitis or Lyme disease
PMH: note recent drugs, especially antibiotics and anticonvulsants; note family history of atopy.

Key dermatologic history questions: duration, evolution/change in appearance, initial vs. current location, associated symptoms (itch/sting/tenderness/pain), family history of similar rash, prior episodes and treatment response, suspected cause per parent, new exposures (meds, personal care products, occupational/recreational), impact on child's life, prior treatments tried.

Additional history: acute/chronic medical conditions; current & recent medications (incl. OTC/herbal); family history of skin disorders/skin cancer; recent stress; social history (daycare, hobbies, travel); allergies; pets; age-appropriate STI risk factors.

sections.part: Approach to Skin Evaluation in Children
sections.title: Physical Examination
body: Begin with vital signs, especially checking for fever.
Observe for lethargy, irritability, or distress.
Full skin exam with attention to blistering, vesicles, petechiae, purpura, urticaria, and mucosal involvement.
Evaluate for meningeal signs (nuchal rigidity, Kernig, Brudzinski) if rash + fever — often absent in children < 2 yrs.
Well-appearing children without systemic symptoms are unlikely to have a dangerous disorder.

sections.part: Approach to Skin Evaluation in Children
sections.title: Skin Descriptors (How to Describe a Lesion)
body: Location & distribution: symmetrical/asymmetrical, sun-exposed, flexural/extensor, acral
Erythema: erythematous vs. non-erythematous
Surface features: crusting, rough, smooth, scaly, warty
Type: macule, papule, pustule, vesicle, cyst, ulcer
Color: blue, brown, pink, red, white
Arrangement: single/multiple, discrete, unilateral, generalized, disseminated, grouped, annular, gyrate, dermatomal, linear, serpiginous
Border/shape: well/poorly defined, active edge, round, oval, irregular, pedunculated
Special sites/systemic: scalp, mouth, nails, genitalia, constitutional symptoms

sections.part: Approach to Skin Evaluation in Children
sections.title: Diagnostic Evaluation
body: History and physical are sufficient for most children.
Additional tools: hand lens/dermatoscope, Wood lamp, patch test, culture, scraping (KOH), biopsy.

sections.part: Approach to Skin Evaluation in Children
sections.title: RED FLAGS — When to Worry
body: Blistering or skin sloughing
Diarrhea and/or abdominal pain
Fever with inconsolability or extreme irritability
Mucosal inflammation
Petechiae and/or purpura
Urticaria with respiratory distress

sections.part: Approach to Skin Evaluation in Children
sections.title: Pediatric Clinical Pearls & Take-Home Points
body: Normal child skin: smooth, slightly dry, not oily/clammy; assess temperature symmetrically, compare upper/lower body.
Skin turgor is the best indicator of dehydration.
Most rashes in children are benign; history and exam are usually sufficient. Rash due to serious illness typically has systemic manifestations.

sections.title: Drug Eruptions
body: Know the typical presentation of a drug reaction rash.
Over 50% of drug rashes are morbilliform (erythematous macules/papules resembling measles), 25% urticaria, 10% fixed drug eruption.

Morbilliform: develops after 5–10 days of drug therapy; red macules/papules erupt on extremities, spread centrally to trunk; often asymptomatic but pruritus may be severe; Type IV (cytotoxic T-cell) reaction; resolves in 1 week after stopping the drug.

Amoxicillin rash: non-immune mediated; up to 10% of children on amoxicillin develop it (up to 5% recurrence risk with re-exposure); appears ~day 5 (up to day 16); lasts ~3 days (1–6 range); body-wide morbilliform pattern.
Fixed drug eruption: reddish/purplish round-oval patches or plaques (± blisters) anywhere on the body; recurs in the same spot with re-exposure; mild itching, burning/pain if blistered.

sections.title: Urticaria & Angioedema
body: Define urticaria and its cardinal sign; define angioedema and its presentation.

Urticaria: a vascular skin reaction with wheals surrounded by a red halo from swelling in the upper dermis. ~15% of children under 10 have ≥1 episode. Cardinal symptom = pruritus. Erythema blanches with pressure. Lesions appear in minutes, enlarge, then resolve.

Angioedema: swelling of the deep dermis/subcutaneous tissue, commonly face (lips, cheeks, periorbital); painful/burning, usually not pruritic; may last several days. Can occur with or without urticaria.
Urticaria can be the cutaneous presentation of anaphylaxis — always assess cardiac/respiratory status.
What is the major immunological response of urticaria?
The mast cell is the major effector.
Immunologic: antigen binds IgE on mast cells → degranulation → histamine release → binds H1/H2 receptors → arteriolar dilation, venous constriction, ↑ capillary permeability → swelling and itch.
Non-immunologic: not IgE-dependent; physical stimuli cause direct mast cell degranulation; drugs cause pharmacologic histamine release.
Common causes of urticaria in children (acute vs. chronic).

Acute: idiopathic (~50%); in children, viral infection is the most common cause (URI, strep, sinusitis, dental abscess, mononucleosis); food reactions (shellfish, nuts, fruit, egg, milk, soy, wheat); drug reactions.
Chronic (rare in children, lasting > 6 weeks): inducible (pressure, cold, heat, water/aquagenic, sunlight/solar, vibration, exercise), autoimmune, chronic infection.
Clinical presentation of (acute) urticaria.
Location anywhere; round/oval shape; pink to red; may coalesce into large raised erythematous areas; transient and migratory; clears within 24 hrs or up to several days.

Wheal duration hints at cause: common (viral/food/drug) 2–24 hrs; contact (latex) < 2 hrs; physical (heat/cold/water/UV) < 1 hr; urticarial vasculitis: several days (a red flag for a different process).
Unlike most pruritic dermatoses, urticarial pruritus rarely leads to excoriations.
What susceptibility do you address when treating urticaria?
Naturopathic approach: first establish etiology → treat the cause (remove allergen/heavy metal/infection/drug) → treat the susceptibility (e.g., leaky gut, stress).
Anti-histamine herbs and nutrients for urticaria.

Botanicals: Glycyrrhiza glabra (anti-inflammatory), Urtica dioica (antihistamine), Curcuma (anti-inflammatory), Lavandula (nervine/anti-inflammatory), Melissa (nervine), Camellia sinensis (antihistamine & anti-inflammatory). For significant inflammation: Plantago, Althea, Arctium lappa, Taraxacum.

Nutrients: L-glutamine 1000 mg BID (adjust for age), NAC, Vitamin C (↓ histamine secretion), Quercetin 250–500 mg BID, Omega-3s, Probiotics 5–10 billion/day, Magnesium (↓ histidine→histamine conversion), DAO enzyme with meals for food intolerance.

Topical/other: herbal baths (Stellaria media, Symphytum, chamomile, calendula + oatmeal/baking soda/Epsom salt); compresses/aloe with frankincense, roman chamomile, peppermint; Gotu cream, Wild Weed salve, Neem cream; NB-UVB for recurrent/chronic hives; low-histamine/anti-inflammatory diet; correct bowel regularity (constipation → liver congestion/toxin recirculation).
Conventional comparison: H1 antihistamines first-line (diphenhydramine, hydroxyzine, cetirizine) ± H2 (ranitidine); topical/oral steroids; identify/avoid triggers; ER referral for anaphylaxis signs.
Homeopathic remedies for acute urticaria (know keynotes).
Apis mellifica: rosy-red, puffy, edematous, stinging/burning; worse heat, better cold/open air.
Arsenicum album: from shellfish; burning/itching with restlessness; worse after midnight; anxious, fear of death.
Belladonna: acute, red hot face/eruptions; worse AM/PM, better scratching.
Histaminum: general allergy/hives remedy.
Medusa: urticaria/prickly heat with burning, lentil-shaped eruptions; impending angioedema (puffy eyes/face, speech difficulty).
Pulsatilla: with diarrhea, worse at night, chilly, weepy/clingy.
Rhus toxicodendron: vesicular, from getting wet/cold; burning, worse cold, better warmth.
Sulphur: worse night/bed/scratching/bathing; nervous, warm, plethoric temperament.
Urtica urens: from shellfish/bee sting; erythematous blotches, worse cold air/water, better lying down.

sections.title: Erythema Nodosum
body: Clinical presentation and etiology of erythema nodosum.
Most common panniculitis in children, usually adolescents — deep-seated, poorly defined, violaceous nodules.
May follow a 1–3 week prodrome (weight loss, malaise, low-grade fever, cough, arthralgia).
Most common trigger in children: β-hemolytic streptococcus.
Sudden-onset erythematous, firm, painful nodules/plaques 1–5 cm, mainly on extensor surfaces of the legs (also arms/thighs, rarely trunk/face).
Relatively benign, favorable course; fades over weeks without scarring.

sections.title: Henoch–Schönlein Purpura (HSP) / IgA Vasculitis
body: Clinical presentation and etiology of HSP.
Most common leukocytoclastic vasculitis in children; often follows a bacterial/viral URI; peak age 4–8 years.
Palpable purpura, 2–10 mm, on buttocks and extensor surfaces of arms/legs.
Joint pain/swelling (knees, ankles) often precedes the rash.
Crops erupt episodically over 2–4 weeks; individual lesions fade in 3–5 days; recurrences in ~half of children over months.
Most managed at home; hospitalize for progressive renal disease or severe abdominal pain.

sections.title: Erythema Multiforme
body: Clinical presentation and etiology of erythema multiforme.
Hypersensitivity reaction, most commonly triggered by HSV-1 infection; next most common trigger Mycoplasma pneumoniae; also medications (NSAIDs, anticonvulsants, sulfonamides).
Sharply demarcated round pink/red macules → raised papules → enlarge into plaques; cutaneous targetoid lesions, mainly face/extremities; may involve mucous membranes.
Systemic symptoms: malaise, arthralgia, muscular stiffness, fever; vision symptoms (dry/bloodshot eyes, eye pain/itch/burn) may occur.
Seen in adolescents/young adults, male predominance; acute and self-limiting.

sections.title: Naturopathic Considerations: EN / HSP / EM
body: Anti-inflammatory diet, adequate hydration.
Nutrients: Zinc, Vitamin A, Vitamin C, Probiotics.
Medicinal mushrooms: Shitake, Reishi, Chaga.
Botanicals: Astragalus, Echinacea, Glycyrrhiza, Ocimum sanctum (holy basil), Curcuma longa, Zingiber.
Warming Sock Treatment or constitutional hydrotherapy (without stimulation).

sections.title: Hand-Foot-Mouth Disease & Herpangina
body: Clinical presentation and etiology of Hand-Foot-Mouth Disease & Herpangina.
HFMD: Coxsackie A5, A10, A16; preschool/school age; highly contagious; incubation 4–6 days; prodrome 1–2 days (low fever, sore throat, malaise).

HFMD exanthem progression: bright pink macules/papules → painful vesicles with erythematous halo → erosions. Enanthem: erosions resembling aphthae. Distribution: starts in mouth (tongue, buccal mucosa, hard palate), then hands/feet ± buttocks, diaper area, thighs, arms.

Herpangina: also Coxsackie; same at-risk group, contagiousness, incubation; prodrome (low fever, anorexia, malaise, sore mouth, dysphagia). Lesions confined to posterior oropharynx (anterior pharyngeal pillars, uvula, soft palate, tonsils): erythematous macules → papules → 2–12 small vesicles that ulcerate centrally with an erythematous halo. Presents like HFMD but oral only.
Conventional management (both): cold compresses, warm salt water rinse, acetaminophen/ibuprofen.

sections.title: Herpes Simplex Virus (Oral)
body: Common cause of oral lesions in toddlers/school-age children; abrupt fever, irritability, inability to eat/drink, tender submandibular/cervical adenopathy.
Vesicular lesions on tongue, buccal mucosa, palate ± lips/face; painful, may persist 10–14 days; can auto-inoculate to hands.
Confirmed by Tzanck smear or viral culture. Topical antivirals have little use in uncomplicated cases.
Naturopathic goals for HFMD / Herpangina / HSV presentations.
Goals: reduce inflammation, support healthy immune response, manage pain.
Diet: easily digestible, cool foods; fluids (filtered water, coconut water, herbal teas) — prone to dehydration from anorexia.
Nutrients: medicinal mushrooms (cordyceps, shitake), Vitamin C, Zinc, Vitamin D, quercetin, grapefruit seed extract.
Botanicals: Astragalus, Arctium lappa, Rubus idaeus, Althea, Eschscholzia californica, Achillea millefolium, Echinacea, Glycyrrhiza, Nepeta cataria.
Warming Sock Treatment/constitutional hydrotherapy; topical antiviral: organic unfiltered honey, Wild Weed salve + diluted peppermint oil; Ayurvedic mouthwash/PerioBrite diluted.

sections.title: Varicella (Chickenpox)
body: Clinical presentation and etiology of varicella.
Varicella zoster virus; at-risk: young/non-immune children; sporadic seasonality; incubation 10–21 days; infectious 2 days before to 5 days after rash onset (respiratory droplets + vesicle fluid).
Prodrome: asymptomatic to fever/malaise/cough/coryza/sore throat.
Rash: widespread "starry sky" distribution; 4 exanthem stages: maculopapular → maculovesicular → ruptures → scabs — all stages can be present at once.
"Dew drop on a rose petal" appearance; thin, easily broken vesicles; heals in 3–5 days then scabs; mild-intense pruritus.
Lab: PCR of viral DNA (most sensitive); DFA; viral culture (highly specific, slow).
Naturopathic treatment goals for varicella.
Goals: control itching, reduce inflammation, support immune response, prevent secondary bacterial infection.
Therapeutic bath: oatmeal/baking soda/Epsom salt ± yarrow + althea.
Topical: cooling paste (equal parts oatmeal + baking soda + water + peppermint EO); calendula/calamine/Florasone lotion; Manuka honey directly on scabs.
Antiviral immune herbs: Echinacea, lemon balm, licorice, astragalus. Immune foods: garlic, ginger, medicinal mushrooms, bone broth. Nutrients: Vitamin C, bioflavonoids, zinc, beta carotene.
Homeopathy 200C potency; Rhus tox for prophylaxis after exposure; Variolinum as homeoprophylaxis.
Three main homeopathic remedies for varicella discussed in class.
Pulsatilla: milder rash, very itchy; weepy/clingy child; worse warmth/stuffy rooms, better cool air; thirstless.
Rhus toxicodendron: intense itching, worse from scratching, relieved by warm baths/heat; restless; sticky inflamed eyes.
Sulfur: red, itchy, burning rash; can't stop scratching; worse warmth/after bathing; drowsy afternoon, hot/restless at night.

Other options mentioned: Antimonium tartaricum (thick yellow fluid, sweaty/fussy), Apis mellifica (pink, puffy, stinging, worse heat), Mezereum (intense itch/burn, face/scalp), Urtica urens (stinging/burning, worse exertion/heat).

sections.title: Impetigo
body: Clinical presentation and etiology of non-bullous and bullous impetigo.

Superficial bacterial infection, ages 2–5 most common; S. aureus or S. pyogenes (GAS); two types: non-bullous (70%) and bullous (30%); very contagious (direct/indirect contact - towels, razors, gym equipment).
General progression: papules → vesicles/pustules/bullae → rupture → honey-colored crust.

Non-bullous: caused by S. aureus (80%) & S. pyogenes (10%); flat, thick, honey-colored crust; usually face (around nose/mouth), can be anywhere; itchy not usually painful; local lymphadenopathy possible, usually no fever. Diagnosis by culture (r/o MRSA). Potential complication: poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis 1–2 weeks post-infection.

Bullous: caused by toxin-mediated S. aureus; summer/humid months; superficial flaccid vesicles → large sharply-marginated bullae without surrounding erythema → rupture to moist red erosions with a collarette of blister roof → honey-colored crust. Affects face, extremities, intertriginous areas (axillae, neck, diaper area). Constitutional symptoms rare/mild. Heals without scarring. Consider CA-MRSA if severe/rapidly progressing.
DDx non-bullous: varicella, scabies, HSV, cutaneous candidiasis. DDx bullous: bullous fixed drug eruption, bullous insect bites.

Conventional: topical mupirocin or retapamulin BID x5d; dilute bleach baths; oral antibiotics for widespread/systemic disease (cephalexin, erythromycin; clindamycin for MRSA); antibacterial soap; UV light.

Naturopathic — Systemic: Echinacea, Berberis aquifolium, Hydrastis, Galium; zinc, Vit A/C, probiotics, garlic 500–1000mg. Topical: Hydrastis powder ± calendula oil, goldenseal-myrrh compound, Allimax gel, Glycyrrhiza or manuka honey, St. John's wort + calendula washes, Epsom salt bath.

sections.title: Folliculitis, Furuncles & Carbuncles
body: Clinical presentation of folliculitis.

Infection of one or more hair follicles; higher risk with diabetes/weak immune system; occurs where rubbing/sweating occur (neck, face, armpits, waist, groin, thighs, buttocks); S. aureus most common cause.
Presentation: red papules/pustules on an inflamed base — warm, swollen, painful. Furuncles uncommon in childhood, more common in puberty. May leave post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation.

sections.title: MRSA Skin Infections
body: How does MRSA present and how is it treated?
Presents as a furuncle/carbuncle: erythematous, swollen, warm, painful, pus-filled/draining ± fever. Can spread systemically and be fatal.
Resistant to penicillin-family antibiotics. Treatment: topical mupirocin (Bactroban); oral TMP-SMX, clindamycin, or tetracycline.

sections.title: Naturopathic Treatment — Skin Infections (Impetigo/Folliculitis/MRSA)
body: Systemic: Echinacea, Rosmarinus, Neem, Hydrastis, Thyme, Astragalus; zinc, Vit A/C, probiotics, allicin, EGCG; omega-3s; liver support (Silybum, Taraxacum, Cynara, Arctium, Rumex, Mahonia).

Topical: Hydrastis + green tea/calendula in aloe; 1:3 apple cider vinegar:water wash; alternating hot/cold Epsom compresses; antimicrobial then heating compress to "bring to a head"; acne-line products (Kamedis, Mother Dirt, Alba, Acure).

sections.title: Week 1, Set 2 — Viral Exanthems
body: Exanthem = an abruptly appearing rash affecting several skin areas at once (Greek "a breaking out"); often "morbilliform." Enanthem = eruption on a mucous membrane. Viral exanthems are more common in children and can be hard to distinguish from drug eruptions — a thorough history is essential.

sections.title: Measles (Rubeola)
body: AKA "14-day measles"; Paramyxovirus. At risk: unvaccinated infants/preschoolers, or school-age children with vaccine failure. Season: late winter/spring. Incubation 8–12 days. Infectious 4 days before to 4 days after rash.

3 clinical stages: (1) Incubation 8–12 days, minimal symptoms; (2) Prodromal/catarrhal (day 7–11): 3–5 days toxic-appearing fever/malaise + the 4 "C/K"s — cough, conjunctivitis, coryza, and enanthem Koplik spots (blue-white "grains of salt" with red halo on buccal mucosa, appear during prodrome, last 2 days into rash); (3) Exanthem: spiking fever, rash begins within 24 hrs of Koplik spots, cephalocaudal spread — starts at hairline, spreads to trunk/extremities, becomes confluent; reddish → dark red-brown as it resolves; lasts ~8 days; skin may peel/flake.
Self-limiting 10–12 days uncomplicated; major cause of infant mortality in developing nations.
Complications: higher risk in pregnancy, young/old, immunocompromised, malnourished. Common: otitis media, pneumonia, croup, diarrhea. Less common: encephalitis, hepatitis, thrombocytopenia.

sections.title: Rubella (German Measles)
body: AKA "3-day measles"; togavirus (only togavirus causing significant human disease); at risk: unvaccinated children/adolescents. Season: late winter/early spring. Incubation 14–21 days. Infectious 1 week before to 1 week after rash.
~50% asymptomatic. Prodrome absent/mild (low fever, headache, sore throat, rhinorrhea, cough) + cervical lymphadenopathy.
Exanthem: pruritic pink-red macules, begin on face, spread to neck/trunk/extremities within 24 hrs; lasts ~3 days. Enanthem: Forchheimer spots (20%).
Complications: peripheral neuritis, encephalitis, thrombocytopenic purpura, arthralgia/arthritis (all rare).

Congenital rubella syndrome: 1st-trimester infection → miscarriage/stillbirth (vaccine contraindicated in pregnancy). Complications: IUGR, rash, jaundice, hepatosplenomegaly, cardiac defects, meningoencephalitis, microcephaly, developmental delay, purpura, deafness. Classic triad: cataracts, cardiac abnormalities (PDA), deafness.

sections.title: Scarlet Fever (Scarlatina)
body: "Rash of strep throat" — due to erythrogenic exotoxin-producing group A β-hemolytic strep (S. pyogenes); diagnosed by rapid antigen test or culture. At risk: <10 yrs, peak 4–8 yrs. Season: late fall/winter/spring. Incubation 2–4 days.
Signs: abrupt fever, headache, vomiting, malaise, sore throat, anterior cervical lymphadenopathy, abdominal pain, desquamation.
Exanthem: "sandpaper rash" — 1–2 mm confluent red papules, starts on neck, moves to trunk then extremities; hot spots: groin, axilla, neck.
Enanthem: bright red oral mucosa, palatal petechiae, "strawberry tongue," exudative pharyngitis, swollen tonsils.
Complications: purulent (otitis media, sinusitis, peritonsillar/retropharyngeal abscess, cervical adenitis); non-suppurative sequela = rheumatic fever.

Conventional Tx: antipyretic/analgesic + antibiotics (do not prevent rash/fever, treat the strep): Penicillin VK 250–500mg BID x10d; Amoxicillin 50mg/kg QD x10d (or 25mg/kg BID); Azithromycin 12mg/kg QD x5d.

sections.title: Erythema Infectiosum (Fifth Disease)
body: Human parvovirus B19; typically age 4–10 (can occur at any age). Season: late winter/early spring. Transmission: respiratory, blood exposure, mother-to-fetus. Incubation 1–2 weeks.
Over 50% asymptomatic. Prodrome: low fever, malaise, headache, pruritus, myalgias; lymphadenopathy absent.

Exanthem: "slapped cheek" appearance → papules form plaques → ~2 days later maculopapular rash on trunk/extremities that fades centrally leaving a lacy/reticular appearance. Resolves 5–10 days but can recur with sun/heat/exercise/stress.

Complications: most common cause of transient aplastic crisis in chronic hemolytic anemia (e.g., sickle cell); immunocompromised → chronic erythroid hypoplasia; pregnancy → hydrops fetalis (1–9% fetal death risk), IUGR, effusions — check maternal parvovirus IgG.

sections.title: Roseola Infantum
body: AKA sixth disease / exanthem subitum ("sudden rash"); HHV-6 (less commonly HHV-7); most common exanthem before age 2; peak 6–7 months (range 6–36 mo). Sporadic; transmission unclear. Incubation 1–2 weeks.
Classic pattern: high fever x 3 days that breaks, followed by rash (erythematous macules/papules with white halos); mild URI symptoms; can be complicated by febrile seizures.

sections.title: Non-Specific Viral Exanthems
body: Most childhood exanthems are non-specific and hard to categorize. No discernible prodromal pattern; associated symptoms: fever, headache, myalgia, fatigue, respiratory/GI complaints. No unique lesion morphology/distribution. Resolves in ~1 week without treatment.
Common causes: non-polio enteroviruses; respiratory viruses (adenovirus, rhinovirus, parainfluenza).

sections.title: Naturopathic Interventions — Viral Exanthems

Homeopathy: Aconite, Belladonna, Chamomilla, Ferrum phos, Phosphorus (general); Scarlet fever set: Ailanthus, Belladonna, Rhus tox, Gelsemium, Aconite, Hepar sulph, Pulsatilla, Sulphur, Zincum met, Scarlatinum; Measles: Aconite, Belladonna, Apis, Pulsatilla, Euphrasia, Gelsemium, Zincum met, Morbillinum (post-exposure prophylaxis, 6c TID x3 days).
Lymphatic support: Calendula, Galium. Immune support: Echinacea, Sambucus, Astragalus, Larch, Melissa, Glycyrrhiza, Allium.
Nervines: Matricaria, Nepeta, Lavandula, Humulus, Passiflora. Eye inflammation: Matricaria/Rosa/Euphrasia infusion compress.

Antiviral/immune nutrients: Vitamin A, C, D3, zinc, beta carotene.

sections.title: Measles & Vitamin A
body: Vitamin A deficiency is a recognized risk factor for severe measles; children <5, adults, malnourished/immunodeficient at highest risk of complications.
WHO recommendation: 200,000 IU/day PO x2 days (100,000 IU/day in infants) for children with measles in areas of possible deficiency. Must set a definite cutoff (~2–3 days).
Toxicity: acute in infants 75,000–300,000 IU (bulging fontanelle, anorexia, irritability, vomiting); chronic 18,000–60,000 IU QD x6–8 wks (premature epiphyseal closure/long bone growth retardation).

sections.title: Featured Botanicals & Nutrients
body: Probiotics (Lactobacillus, Bifidobacterium, Saccharomyces boulardii): synthesize SCFAs/B-vitamins/biotin/folate/K, enhance gut motility/nutrient absorption, colonization resistance, stimulate macrophages/NK/monocytes/neutrophils, enhance Ig response to vaccines.

Larch: polysaccharide fiber feeds Bifido/Lacto/Entero → SCFA production; combined with Echinacea has a stronger immune-stimulating effect than either alone; ↑ WBC/cytokine (NK) activity; competitively binds bacterial fimbriae (esp. gram-negatives like E. coli, Klebsiella); dose 1–3 tsp/day; no known toxicity, may cause gas/bloating.
Echinacea: immune-stimulating, antimicrobial, ↑ macrophage activity and secretory immunity; dose 50mg BID.
Astragalus: long-term immune modulator; ↑ TNF-α/β and IFN production; synergistic antiviral activity with elderberry.
Sambucus (elderberry): antiviral, immune-modulating via cytokine stimulation; combined with Echinacea + Vit C for added effect.
Vitamin D3 dosing: infants 400–800 IU; toddlers 1000 IU; children >5: 2000 IU (or 35 IU/lb/day <5yo).
Vitamin C dosing: children <2 yrs 125–250mg QD-BID; 2 yrs+ 250–500mg QD-BID (to bowel tolerance).

sections.title: Pediatric Dosing Formulas
body: Young's Rule (uses age): Child's Dose = Adult Dose × Age ÷ (Age + 12).
Clark's Rule (uses weight in lbs, never kg): Child's Dose = Adult Dose × (Weight ÷ 150).

sections.title: Psoriasis in Children
body: Clinical manifestation/prevalence; triggers; treatment goals; top homeopathic remedies.
Chronic inflammatory disease: well-demarcated erythematous papules/plaques with fine silvery scale.
In children: more pruritic, more common in girls; plaques thinner/softer/less scaly. Intertriginous, facial, and anogenital involvement more common than in adults.
Occurs at any age, most frequent 5–11 years. Under age 2, psoriatic diaper rash is the most common presentation. Scalp is the most frequently involved region (site of onset in 40–60% under age 20).
Guttate psoriasis: seen in children/teens, often follows a streptococcal throat infection.
Triggers: stress, medication, injury, infection.
Treatment goals: combine topical therapy, phototherapy, and oral supplementation (nutrients/botanicals).

Naturopathic — Diet: gluten-free, low-carb/high-protein diets → milder symptoms; vegan/Paleo/Mediterranean may also help. Botanicals: Mahonia aquifolium, Silybum, Arctium lappa, Curcuma longa, Angelica sinensis, Smilax, Matricaria recutita, Trifolium pratense, Scutellaria baicalensis, Rheum palmatum. Nutrients: Vit D/A/C, quercetin, omega-3, EPO. Phototherapy: NB-UVB 3x/week, 10–20 min. Topicals: oat/Dead Sea/Epsom baths + essential oils (pine, fir, tea tree, thyme); sulfur balsam lotion; rose geranium/lavender/sandalwood/frankincense in aloe; apple cider vinegar scalp spray.

Top homeopathic remedies: Arsenicum album (dry/rough/red with silvery scale, spares face/hands, worse cold, guttate psoriasis); Graphites (sore/dry/rough with cracks, nail involvement, scalp scaling behind ears); Petroleum (burning/intolerable itch, deep bleeding cracks); Mercurius solubilis (scalp presentation, abundant white scales, raw base, worse night, sour sweat); also Sulphur (severe itch/burn, worse night/bed), Phosphorus (elbows/knees), Lycopodium (hands).

sections.title: Pityriasis Rosea
body: Clinical presentation and supposed cause of pityriasis rosea.
Mild, common; children ≥10 yrs. Starts with a single 2–10cm oval scaly plaque with raised border and depressed center (herald patch) on chest/stomach/back.

~1–2 weeks later: smaller pink/tan patches spread, classically in a "Christmas tree" pattern on the back; also neck/arms/legs. Occasional mild itch. Papular rash in young children/people of color; vesicular rash possible in infants.
Resolves in 4–6 weeks, up to 1–3 months. Cause unknown, suspected viral (H1N1, COVID-19, HHV-6/7); may be vaccine-triggered (H1N1, diphtheria, smallpox, hep B, pneumococcus, COVID-19).
DDx: tinea corporis, tinea versicolor, eczema, psoriasis. Self-resolving; sunlight may help.

sections.title: Acne Vulgaris
body: Manifestations, dietary recommendations, probiotic strains.
Affects up to 85% of adolescents; rare in infancy (6wk–1yr); male teen predominance. Preadolescent (7–12yo) acne often the first sign of puberty, usually comedonal in a T-zone distribution.
4 processes: (1) sebaceous hyperplasia (↑ androgens), (2) altered follicular growth/differentiation, (3) follicular colonization by P. acnes, (4) immune response/inflammation.

3 morphologies: comedonal (open/closed), inflammatory (papules/pustules/nodules/pseudocysts), mixed. Severity: mild <20 comedones/<15 inflam./<30 total; moderate 20–100/15–50/30–125; severe >100 comedones/>50 inflam./>5 pseudocysts/>125 total.

Dietary recommendations: address leaky gut/food intolerances; ↑ milk consumption and high-glycemic-load diets associated with adolescent acne — remove sugar, dairy, and whey protein; anti-inflammatory diet.
Liver support: Burdock, Oregon grape, yellow dock, Taraxacum root. Anti-inflammatory botanicals: Stellaria media, Urtica dioica, Trifolium pratense, Achillea millefolium, chamomile, Zingiber.
Supplements: Vit D & A, zinc, EFAs, Vit C, Vit B5, selenium, EGCG, curcumin, resveratrol.
Probiotic strains: Lactobacillus plantarum (↑ collagen synthesis, hydration, tone, UV protection), Bifidobacterium lactis, Lactobacillus acidophilus.

sections.title: Keratosis Pilaris
body: Define keratosis pilaris, its clinical manifestation, and treatment.
A benign follicular keratinization disorder — small rough, folliculocentric papules ("chicken skin"), commonly on upper arms/thighs/cheeks.

Treatment: Omega-3s, Vit D & A; remove sugar/dairy/gluten from diet; probiotics (Thera-Biotic, Nordic Naturals gummies); 2:1 filtered water:apple cider vinegar topical; lactic acid exfoliation (yogurt/kefir + brown sugar + coconut oil weekly); lactic-acid topical products (e.g., DRMTLGY).

sections.title: Fungal Infections
body: Most common fungal infections in children; presentation of tinea capitis, transmission, kerion; tinea pedis/corporis; pityriasis versicolor; probiotic strains for tinea.
Tinea capitis is the most common dermatological disorder in school-age children (Trichophyton tonsurans). Diaper candidiasis is the most common in infants.
KOH exam limitations: small/unaffected sample, prior antifungal treatment causes false negatives; false negatives more common with KOH than culture.

Tinea capitis: dermatophytosis of scalp/hair; spread by direct contact with animals/humans/fomites (shared brushes, combs, caps, helmets, pillows). Non-inflammatory (black dot) or inflammatory (kerion), or both. Presentation: hair loss, scaling, erythema, itch, crusting; postauricular/posterior cervical/occipital lymphadenopathy; broken hairs prominent.
Kerion = a painful, inflammatory, boggy mass with broken hair follicles; untreated tinea capitis can progress here; may look bacterial (pus present); can scar — refer immediately to dermatology.

Tx: topicals ineffective alone (can use antifungal shampoo adjunctively); griseofulvin (old standby, best for Microsporum, 20–25 mg/kg q24h x8wk) or terbinafine (best for Trichophyton tonsurans, weight-based dosing x4–8wk).
Tinea pedis: adolescents; fine white scaly plaque, erythema, pruritic, macerated skin, tense bullae.
Tinea corporis: annular configuration, erythema, fine scaly plaques, often pruritic; mainly ages 2–10.

Pityriasis (tinea) versicolor: overgrowth of Malassezia furfur (normal flora); pityriasiform desquamation with hypo/hyperpigmented macules, mostly face/neck/back; worsens with heat/humidity/steroids/immunosuppression; mostly adolescence.

Conventional tinea tx: topical allylamines (terbinafine, naftifine — shorter course) or imidazoles (clotrimazole, miconazole — less expensive); antifungal washes (ketoconazole 2%, selenium sulfide 2.5%, zinc pyrithione).

Naturopathic tinea tx: systemic immune support (garlic, neem, turmeric); antifungals (grapefruit seed extract, oil of oregano, caprylic acid); probiotics: Saccharomyces boulardii, Lactobacillus acidophilus, L. reuteri, L. plantarum; botanicals (berberine, Mahonia, Rumex, silymarin, Usnea, calendula); topical coconut oil, aloe + EOs (bitter orange, tea tree, Siberian fir, thyme, oregano), herbal astringents (Hamamelis, Achillea, chamomile, geranium, Camellia sinensis).
Refer: tinea pedis/corporis/cruris failing hygiene + antifungal therapy, large BSA involved, or atypical body areas.

sections.title: Seborrheic Dermatitis ("Cradle Cap")
body: Cause and common location of seborrheic dermatitis in infants.
Infants: most common on scalp, also behind ears, neck creases, axillae, diaper area (adults: face, eyebrows, scalp, chest).

Fine white scale to erythematous plaques with greasy yellowish scale; may cause hypopigmentation. Thought to be an inflammatory reaction to Malassezia spp. (normal flora) plus increased sebaceous activity.

Treatment: scalp rinse — infusion of Trifolium pratense + Viola tricolor + Arctium lappa seed, once daily after brushing; scalp oil — olive/argan oil + lavender/tea tree/rosemary or basil EO applied at bedtime, rinsed with calendula shampoo, crust removed gently.

sections.title: Diaper Dermatitis
body: Classifications, precipitating conditions, clinical presentation, conventional and naturopathic treatment.

One of the most common infant/child skin conditions; related to chafing/irritation from urine/stool exposure, infrequent changes, food sensitivities, solid food introduction, antibiotic use. Fecal enzymes activated by urine alkalinity damage skin.

Classifications: irritant/contact ("ammoniacal" dermatitis from diaper environment); inflammatory (seborrheic derm, atopic derm, infantile psoriasis exacerbated by diaper environment); nutritional deficiency (most commonly zinc); infectious (Candida albicans most common).

Diaper candidiasis: beefy red confluent patches/plaques/erosions with marginal scaling over buttocks/genitals/thighs; satellite papules/pustules differentiate it from other diaper eruptions; KOH/culture confirms. Suspect when unresponsive to barrier creams (zinc oxide, petroleum, triple paste).

Conventional Tx: nystatin cream/ointment; clotrimazole/miconazole; Triple Paste AF (zinc oxide 40% + miconazole); oral nystatin if oral thrush/recurrent; add 1% hydrocortisone short-term if very inflamed.

Naturopathic: prevention with ointment barriers (better than creams; powders controversial); topical herbal creams (calendula, chamomile, probiotic); zinc oxide or sea buckthorn barrier creams; bentonite clay dusting; gentian violet (stains clothing) x10–14 days; review breastfeeding mother's diet (elimination/candida diet); infant/maternal probiotics; B vitamins/Vit D (possible antifungal effect); clove oil (eugenol) shown as effective as nystatin.

sections.title: Pityriasis Alba
body: Clinical presentation, stages, and resolution of pityriasis alba.
Benign, common, self-resolving eczematous rash of unknown cause; ages 3–16, equal in boys/girls; may associate with atopy (eczema, asthma, hay fever).
Round/oval/irregular patches or thin plaques with poorly defined edges on cheeks, chin, neck, shoulders, upper arms.
3 stages: (1) slightly scaly pink patch/plaque, (2) hypopigmented patch with fine scale, (3) post-inflammatory hypopigmented macules without scale prior to resolution.
Resolves over ~1 year on average (a few months up to 2–3 years). Hypopigmentation more visible in summer; dryness/scaling more visible in winter.
Distinguished from pityriasis versicolor by KOH exam — fungal elements present in versicolor, not in alba.

sections.title: Atopic Dermatitis
body: Clinical presentation; hygiene hypothesis; triggers.
"Eczema" = generic term for inflammatory skin condition. 10–15% of infants have a family history of the atopic triad (asthma, allergic rhinitis, eczema).

Pathophysiology: abnormal Th1/Th2 balance, elevated IgE, eosinophilia, defective skin barrier (filaggrin gene variant), reduced innate immune response. Intense pruritus with exacerbation/remission course.
Hygiene hypothesis: reduced early-life microbial exposure may impair immune tolerance development, contributing to rising atopic disease.

Presentation by stage: acute — pruritic erythematous papules/vesicles over erythematous skin, excoriations/erosions with serous exudate; subacute — erythema, excoriation, scaling; chronic — thickened plaques, lichenification, fibrotic papules.

Location by age: nonmobile infant — face/scalp; crawling infant — extensor extremities, trunk, face, neck; older child/adolescent — wrists, ankles, antecubital/popliteal fossae, neck. Follicular pattern more common in darker skin types.

Triggers: dry skin/low humidity, irritants (wool, perfumes, soaps, laundry detergent), phthalates (cosmetics, food packaging, vinyl toys), stress, allergens (cow's milk, peanuts, almonds, sesame, egg, corn, soy, gluten, citrus), infections (bacterial/viral/fungal), heat and sweat.

sections.title: Discoid (Nummular) Eczema
body: Clinical presentation of discoid eczema.

Common in children/young adults; round, coin-like red patches on arms/legs. Two forms: dry (redness + scaly, common) and wet (oozing/crusting). Frequently mistaken for tinea corporis. Slow to resolve.

sections.title: Eczema — Treatment
body: Conventional: antihistamines (diphenhydramine, fexofenadine, loratadine, ketotifen); topical steroids (hydrocortisone, desonide, triamcinolone, mometasone, betamethasone); NB-UVB; topical calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus, pimecrolimus) when steroids ineffective; topical crisaborole (PDE4 inhibitor).

Naturopathic topicals: barrier moisturizers (Kamedis, Graham's, California Baby, Dr. Bronner's Magic balm, neem leaf & aloe, sea buckthorn salve, Florasone); topical probiotic sprays/creams (Mary Ruth's, LiviaOne, Siani BabyBiotics, AllVia).
Hydrotherapy: bathe daily/every 2–3 days, soap only 2–3x/week; oatmeal/Epsom/sea salt baths; wet sheet packs for widespread disease; constitutional hydrotherapy.

Diet: whole-foods anti-inflammatory diet; eliminate cow dairy, soy, egg, gluten/wheat; kefir/fermented veggies (L. paracasei, L. fermentum); healthy fats (fish, flax, hemp, olive, coconut, avocado); EFA 800mg EPA/day; Vit A/C/D/E, zinc.
Vitamin A: only if other treatments have been ineffective; ages 6mo–10yr, 5,000–10,000 IU/day for 1–2 months.

Botanicals: Matricaria recutita, Urtica dioica, Hibiscus rosa-sinensis, Trifolium pratense, Arctium lappa, Stellaria media, Azadirachta indica. Medicinal mushrooms: Chaga (skin repair/sun protection), Shitake (antioxidant), Tremella (moisturizer).
Immune modulators: probiotics 10–50 billion CFU (acidophilus, bifidobacterium, S. boulardii); Vit D 400–1000 IU QD; Echinacea, Astragalus, Hydrastis/Berberis, Glycyrrhiza.

Anti-inflammatories: Vit C 125–200mg QD-BID (to bowel tolerance); bioflavonoids 100–250mg BID; EPA+DHA 200–1500mg QD; quercetin 120–250mg BID; bromelain 50–250mg BID away from meals; resveratrol 150–300mg QD; Curcuma longa, Scutellaria baicalensis, Camellia sinensis, Rheum palmatum; NB-UVB, red LED, natural sunlight.
Three homeopathic remedies for children with eczema (know keynotes).
Graphites: dry/rough with scaling OR wet with sticky transparent discharge; cracks; bends of elbows/knees, face, neck, behind ears; severe itching.
Sulphur: excessively dry, scaly, intolerable itch; worse night/warmth of bed; burning after scratching; top remedy if condition has been suppressed (e.g., after steroid suppression).
Rhus tox: marked burning/intense itch; thick oozing crusts; red skin, worse from scratching; vesicular bumps possible.

Other options: Petroleum (dry, cracked, bleeding, crusted, burning), Natrum muriaticum (bends of limbs, worse warmth, scalp margin/hairline crusting), Arsenicum album (dry/rough/scaly, face, worse night), Mezereum (sticky oozing, worse warm bathing, infant scalp), Histaminum hydrochloricum (allergic burning/itching/redness).

sections.title: Verruca Vulgaris (Warts / HPV)
body: Define verruca vulgaris and common ages; types of HPV on skin; vitamin deficiencies; class remedies.

Cutaneous lesions from HPV invading epithelial cells, causing benign epithelial tumors. Incubation weeks to years. Most common ages 12–16 (10–20% prevalence). Transmission: skin-to-skin, mucous membrane contact, fomites.

Types: Common — around nails/back of hands, rough surface, grayish-yellow/brown; Flat — small smooth growths in groups, pink/tan/yellow, often on face; Filiform — small, long, narrow, on eyelids/face/neck; Plantar — soles of feet, black dots (clotted vessels), clusters called "mosaic," may be painful.
Most warts resolve without treatment over time. Conventional: salicylic acid, liquid nitrogen, podophyllin, electrocautery, cantharidin, H2O2 40%, laser.

Naturopathic: oral Vitamin D, Zinc, Vitamin B12, NAC; botanicals (Astragalus, Melissa officinalis, Echinacea purpurea, Ganoderma lucidum); topical (aspirin, Vit C, or apple cider vinegar/baking soda poultice, pineapple juice soaks, thuja oil, garlic, castor oil, banana peel for plantar); duct tape occlusion (apply 1–3 days, remove, abrade with pumice, repeat).
Remedies used to treat verruca vulgaris in children discussed during lecture.
Thuja occidentalis: most common remedy for warts of all kinds — isolated jagged warts that bleed easily, or mosaic plantar warts.
Causticum: old, pedunculated warts, very touch-sensitive; hard/horny, bleed easily; especially warts on the head.
Nitric acidum: large, fissured, itchy/stinging/bleeding-on-washing warts; horny wall around a central depression; common plantar wart remedy.

Others: Antimonium crudum (hard smooth warts in groups, white coated tongue), Calcarea carbonica (fleshy/horny/painful, chilly child), Dulcamara (flat/hard, hands/face, worse cold/damp), Ferrum picricum (small pointed, groups), Graphites (periungual/corn-like, tinged yellow), Natrum muriaticum (palms/fingers, salt cravings).

sections.part: Week 3 — Nodules, Tumors, Hair/Nail Disorders & Infestations
sections.title: Molluscum Contagiosum
body: Define molluscum contagiosum and common ages; clinical presentation; class remedies.

Pox virus; incubation 2–7 weeks. <5% of US children have evidence of infection, though it's a common childhood disease. Occurs in healthy individuals, most prevalent in school-age children. Common locations: face, armpits, arms. Transmission: fomites, close contact, autoinoculation (common in the anogenital region in children).

Presentation: small, flesh-colored, dome-shaped, umbilicated papules, very discrete; occasional rim of inflammation; cheesy material may express from lesions. Full body exam recommended. Diagnosis by appearance; histology (H&E) shows Henderson-Patterson bodies.
Treatment goals: limit spread, reduce transmission risk, reduce pruritus, prevent scarring from secondary infection.
Conventional: low/medium potency topical steroid if pruritic; podofilox (not established safe <10 yrs); cryotherapy; curettage; cantharidin.

Naturopathic: watchful waiting advised (may last months–years untreated); procedures (curettage, liquid nitrogen, salicylic acid); essential oils (Australian lemon myrtle, thuja, tea tree, neem); topicals (apple cider vinegar + baking soda poultice, raw/manuka honey, colloidal oatmeal + zinc oxide); commercial preps (Zymaderm, Naturasil, Emuaid).
Remedies used to treat molluscum contagiosum discussed during lecture.
Thuja: eruptions only on covered parts/anogenital region; worse after scratching; very touch-sensitive; chilly.
Natrum muriaticum: around eyes/mouth, irregular shape, burns in skin folds; dry, scaly, unhealthy skin.
Calcarea carbonica: unhealthy skin, hard/large/slow-healing lesions, swollen glands.

Others: Bromium (enlarged glands, weak immunity), Causticum (burning/rawness in skin folds/behind ears/thighs), Kali iodatum (rough nodules, worse heat/covering, very restless), Lycopodium (worse warm applications, sweet cravings), Natrum sulphuricum (worse damp weather), Phosphorus (tendency to bleed, intense thirst), Silicea (umbilicated with offensive pus), Sulphur (voluptuous itching), Tuberculinum (used as intercurrent), Bowel nosodes (Morgan pure, Gaertner).

sections.title: Epidermoid Cysts
body: Define epidermoid cyst and common location in children.
Benign, encapsulated, subepidermal nodule filled with keratin material. Most common orbital/periorbital tumor in the pediatric population; also found on scalp, face, neck, trunk.
Exam: soft, painless mass. Conventional treatment: surgical removal.
Naturopathic: witch hazel or apple cider vinegar poultice; frankincense EO, castor oil, bentonite clay, grapefruit seed extract; oral zinc, Vit A/D/C.

sections.title: Paronychia
body: Acute or chronic inflammation of the lateral/proximal nail folds. S. aureus in acute infection; Streptococci and Pseudomonas more common in chronic infection.
Caused by disruption of the cuticle (protective nail-fold barrier); predisposing factors: overzealous manicuring, nail biting, hangnail picking, thumb sucking, ingrown nail.
Exam: erythematous, swollen, tender lateral nail fold; if abscess present, pressure on the volar digit reveals a larger-than-expected blanching area.
Conventional: I&D or antibiotics; warm soaks/antiseptic solutions if no definite abscess.
Naturopathic: topical salt water/lemon/apple cider vinegar soaks; poultice of neem, turmeric, or garlic; thyme/oregano application; oral Echinacea, Melissa, Glycyrrhiza, Vit C, zinc.

sections.title: Alopecia
body: Common causes of pediatric alopecia; associated conditions; naturopathic interventions.
Most common causes: tinea capitis, alopecia areata, traction alopecia/trichotillomania, telogen effluvium.
Key first step: differentiate hair shedding vs. hair breakage. Associated with hypothyroidism and nutritional deficiency (vitamins/minerals).

Diagnosis: directed history, scalp/hair exam, dermoscopy, basic labs. Exam: visual inspection of distribution/density, part-width measurement, hair shaft length/caliber/fragility/texture; broken/rough hairs suggest a hair-shaft disorder or trauma.

sections.title: Infestations — Lice
body: Symptoms of lice infestation; lice/nit survival off-host; naturopathic interventions.
Tiny wingless parasitic insects feeding on human blood; spread by close contact and sharing belongings. Head lice (pediculosis) most common in preschool/elementary-age children.
Survival off-host: lice survive < 1–2 days without a blood meal; nits usually die within a week if not kept at scalp-proximity temperature.
Symptoms: intense itching, tickling sensation, visible nits/lice, sores, irritability, sleeplessness.
Supplemental measures: machine wash/dry linens & clothing hot; soak combs/brushes in hot water; vacuum floors/furniture where the person sat/lay.
Conventional: OTC pyrethrin (Rid), permethrin 1% (Nix); Rx benzyl alcohol 5%, ivermectin 0.5% lotion, malathion 0.5% lotion, spinosad 0.9% suspension.

Naturopathic: topical EOs (neem, red thyme, eucalyptus, cinnamon leaf, anise in EVOO carrier); daily wet-combing with diluted apple cider vinegar; smothering agents (olive oil, coconut oil, mayonnaise, non-petroleum jelly); hair-dryer diffuser treatment; commercial lines (Head Hunters, Organic Lice Guru professional service).

sections.title: Infestations — Scabies
body: Clinical presentation of Sarcoptes scabiei infection; naturopathic interventions.
Infection by the mite Sarcoptes scabiei; transmitted by close contact (mites survive up to 48 hrs on fomites); uncommon in African Americans.
Life cycle: female burrows into the superficial skin layer to lay eggs; larvae mature over 3–4 weeks then surface to mate; adults cannot survive off the body longer than 2–3 days.

Presentation: rash with severe itching from a delayed Type IV hypersensitivity reaction to mites/feces/eggs; itching often worse at night; papules, nodules, scaling, excoriation, secondary bacterial infection possible; burrows may be seen in finger webs, wrist flexors, axillae, umbilicus, nipples, buttocks, penis.
Conventional: 5% permethrin (Elimite) single application, treat all family members even if asymptomatic; oral ivermectin.
Naturopathic: topical EOs (neem, clove, tea tree, cinnamon, lemongrass) in aloe vera gel; oral Vitamin A; commercial topical lines (Emuaid, Naturasil).

sections.title: VENTRICULAR SEPTAL DEFECT (VSD)
body: Ventricular septum fails to form during embryonic
development. sx may not occur until 1-2 months of life. May
close spontaneously until 4 years of age or remain stable.

sections.title: MITRAL VALVE PROLAPSE (MVP)
body: Most common valvular abnormality. Usually benign, associated
with mitral regurgitation.
PE: mid-to-late systolic click and blowing, holosystolic murmur.
dx confirmed w/ echo.

sections.title: COARCTATION OF THE AORTA (CoA)
body: Congenital narrowing of the aorta. Clinical sx: hypertension,
dyspnea, intermittent claudication, angina, cool extremities,
and headaches.
PE: systolic murmur is typically heard at the LUSB with
radiation to the left inter-scapular area. Significant discrepancy
in blood pressure and pulse amplitude between the upper and
lower extremities.
Cyanotic lesions: ToF and ToGA.

sections.title: TRANSPOSITION OF THE GREAT ARTERIES (ToGA)
body: aorta arises from the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery
arises from the left ventricle —> complete separation of the
pulmonary and systemic circulations.
diagnosis: prenatally via ultrasound. Hours after birth: severe
cyanosis --> referred for surgury: btw days 3 to 5 of life,
delaying surgery 30 days --> myocardial deconditioning.
Treatment: the arterial switch procedure.

sections.title: TETRALOGY OF FALLOT (ToF)
body: Four key features: pulmonary stenosis, RVH, VSD, overriding
aorta. It may be associated with Down syndrome.
“Tet spells”: sudden drop in blood oxygen levels, leading to
increased cyanosis.
Surgical repair: Shunt placement btw the aorta and pulmonary
artery followed by complete intracardiac repair. Definitive
repair: widening the pulmonary outflow tract + closing the VSD.
First cardiac surgery performed on a child: Blalock–Taussig shunt,
developed in 1944 at Johns Hopkins: relieves cyanosis in Tetralogy
of Fallot.

sections.title: Acquired Heart Disease
body: Kawasaki’s Disease (KD): acute, self-limiting vasculitis - occurs in
children 6 months to 5 years of age. Leading cause of acquired
heart disease in the US and Japan.
Timeline of the clinical manifestation of Kawasaki Disease.
Diagnosis: fever lasting five or more days, along with at least
four of the following five:
criteria: bilateral conjunctival injection; changes in the
mucous membranes (injected pharynx, fissured lips, or a
strawberry tongue); changes in the peripheral extremities
(peripheral edema, erythema, and desquamation of the
palms and soles); a polymorphous rash; and cervical LAO.
Cardiac concerns in KD: coronary artery aneurysms - two weeks
after symptom onset. Order an ECHO to assess.
Treatment: high-dose IVIG in combinations with high doses of
aspirin.
Long-term prognosis: Scarring can lead to coronary artery
stenosis ⟶ risk of ischemic heart disease in young adults.
Persistent mitral or aortic regurgitation; premature
atherosclerosis; long-term heart damage.
Rheumatic Fever (RF)
● develops after a GA β HS infection, primarily affecting the mitral
and aortic valves of the heart --> valve damage (usually
regurgitation) --> can cause rheumatic heart disease.
Diagnosis: a recent GA β HS infection AND the presence of two
major criteria OR 1 major criteria plus 2 minor criteria, which
are:
MAJOR CRITERIA: carditis, polyarthritis, chorea, erythema
marginatum, and subcutaneous nodules
MINOR CRITERIA: fever, arthralgia, elevated acute phase
reactants (ESR, CRP), and prolonged PR interval on EKG
Imaging: CXR, ECHO, and EKG.
Treatment: oral penicillin or Penicillin G IM.
PCP role: recognizing and treating streptococcal infections
promptly. Be aware of potential systemic symptoms of
untreated or delayed treatment of a strep infection, which may
not present until weeks after the sore throat has resolved.

sections.title: HYPERTROPHIC CARDIOMYOPATHY

arrhythmias. 2 most common form of heart muscle disease nd
Familial hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: genes encoding

Sx: asymptomatic in most patients; dyspnea with exertion;
Chest pain; Palpitations; blood clots and heart failure;
Syncope during exercise; stroke; sudden death
Murmur: Harsh, crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur
heard at the LLSB, increases Valsalva. Decreases with
squatting
Diagnosis: EKG, ECHO, MRI, stress test, ambulatory EKG
monitoring, and selective coronary angiography. EKG findings
dagger-like Q waves in the lateral leads and a high-amplitude
QRS complex.
Greatest risk: sudden cardiac death.

A period of detraining (6 weeks of minimal exercise) the heart
