protocols.title: Urinary Tract Infection (UTI)
protocols.background: Urinary tract infections (UTIs) are infections that occur anywhere along the urinary tract, most commonly affecting the bladder (cystitis) and urethra (urethritis), and less frequently the kidneys (pyelonephritis). They are primarily caused by ascending bacterial pathogens, most notably Escherichia coli, which accounts for up to 90% of cases. Risk factors include female sex, sexual activity, urinary stasis, catheterization, and anatomical abnormalities. UTIs are highly prevalent, especially among women, with nearly half experiencing at least one episode in their lifetime. Pathophysiologically, bacteria colonize the periurethral area, ascend the urethra, and adhere to uroepithelial cells, triggering inflammation. Clinically, UTIs typically present with dysuria, urinary frequency, urgency, suprapubic discomfort, and hematuria. In upper tract infections, fever, flank pain, and systemic symptoms may occur. Differential diagnoses include vaginitis, interstitial cystitis, urethritis, and sexually transmitted infections. Diagnosis is based on clinical symptoms and confirmed with urinalysis and urine culture. Management involves increased fluid intake and appropriate antibiotics, with nitrofurantoin or TMP-SMX commonly used for uncomplicated cases. Prognosis is generally excellent with timely treatment, but complications such as recurrent infections, renal scarring, or sepsis can occur, particularly in high-risk groups like pregnant women and the elderly.

steps.dose: 2 grams three times daily for 5-7 days
steps.why: D-Mannose inhibits bacterial adhesion, particularly of E. coli, to the bladder wall, helping flush pathogens out through urination. It's effective for acute symptom management and recurrent UTI prevention.

steps.dose: 500 mg capsule or 5 mL tincture every 2-3 hours (max 5 days)
steps.why: Contains arbutin, a urinary antiseptic that becomes active in alkaline urine, reducing bacterial load. Best for short-term use due to potential liver toxicity with prolonged dosing.

steps.dose: 500-1000 mg extract TID (acute), or 6-8 oz unsweetened juice TID
steps.why: Rich in proanthocyanidins that prevent bacterial adhesion to the urinary tract lining. Useful in both acute infections and for reducing recurrence risk.

steps.dose: One capsule intravaginally once weekly for 4 weeks
steps.why: Recolonizes the vaginal flora with protective Lactobacilli, helping lower vaginal pH and outcompete uropathogens, especially beneficial in individuals with recurrent UTIs.

Hydration: Encourage >1.5-2 L/day to promote bladder flushing. Avoid Irritants: Limit caffeine, alcohol, and spicy food during active infection. Safety Plan: Educate patients to seek emergent medical care for fever, flank pain, or symptoms >3 days.

protocols.title: Sexually Transmitted Infection (STI)
protocols.background: Sexually transmitted infections (STIs) are infections primarily spread through sexual contact, including vaginal, anal, and oral sex. They are caused by a range of pathogens, including bacteria (eg, Chlamydia trachomatis, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Treponema pallidum), viruses (eg, HIV , HPV , HSV), and parasites (eg, Trichomonas vaginalis). STIs are among the most common infectious diseases worldwide, with young adults aged 15-24 at highest risk due to behavioral and biological factors. Social stigma, limited access to care, and asymptomatic carriers contribute to widespread transmission. Pathophysiologically, pathogens invade mucosal or epithelial surfaces, triggering local and systemic immune responses. Clinical presentations vary but may include urethral or vaginal discharge, dysuria, genital ulcers, pelvic pain, or asymptomatic infection. Differential diagnoses include urinary tract infections, bacterial vaginosis, candidiasis, and dermatologic conditions. Diagnosis is based on history, physical exam, and targeted lab tests (eg, NAATs, serology). Management depends on the pathogen but often includes antibiotics or antivirals, partner notification, and education. Prognosis is generally good with early treatment, but untreated STIs can lead to complications such as pelvic inflammatory disease, infertility, chronic pelvic pain, adverse pregnancy outcomes, and increased HIV risk.

steps.dose: 1+ billion CFU Lactobacillus spp intravaginally once daily for 7-10 days
steps.why: Restores healthy vaginal flora by promoting acid-producing Lactobacilli, which suppress overgrowth of pathogenic bacteria and yeast. Especially effective in BV and yeast infections, and helpful post-antibiotic.

steps.dose: Lysine 3 g/day during outbreaks, 1-2 g/day for prevention
steps.why: Add: Melissa officinalis or Glycyrrhiza glabra tea or tincture (2-4 mL TID) Lysine competes with arginine to inhibit HSV replication. Antiviral herbs further support immune defense and may reduce severity and duration of lesions.

Topical: Sinecatechin 15% ointment, apply TID for up to 16 weeks Oral: 500-800 mg green tea extract daily for 3-6 months EGCG in green tea supports HPV clearance and immune modulation. Topical formulations can reduce size and recurrence of genital warts.

protocols.title: Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD)
protocols.background: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is defined as a gradual, irreversible decline in kidney function lasting more than three months, typically measured by a glomerular filtration rate (GFR) <60 mL/min/1.73 m² and/or evidence of kidney damage such as albuminuria. Major causes include diabetes mellitus, hypertension, glomerulonephritis, and polycystic kidney disease. CKD affects approximately 10-15% of the global population, with increased prevalence in older adults and those with cardiovascular risk factors. Pathophysiologically, CKD involves progressive nephron loss leading to compensatory hyperfiltration, glomerular sclerosis, and interstitial fibrosis. Patients may remain asymptomatic in early stages, with later symptoms including fatigue, edema, hypertension, uremia, and electrolyte imbalances. Differential diagnoses include acute kidney injury, urinary tract obstruction, and nephrotic syndrome. Diagnosis relies on eGFR, urinalysis, albumin-to- creatinine ratio, and renal imaging. Management focuses on slowing progression through blood pressure control (ACE inhibitors/ARBs), glycemic management, lifestyle modifications, and avoidance of nephrotoxins. Prognosis varies by stage and comorbidities; however, advanced CKD can progress to end-stage renal disease requiring dialysis or transplant. Complications include anemia, mineral-bone disorder, cardiovascular disease, and increased mortality.

steps.why: Early CKD: 0.8-1 g/kg/day Moderate to Advanced CKD: 0.6-0.8 g/kg/day Restricting protein slows kidney workload and reduces nitrogenous waste accumulation. Emphasize plant-based proteins like legumes, soy, and quinoa while avoiding red and processed meats.

steps.dose: <2 g/day (or up to 3 g/day if strict restriction not tolerated)
steps.why: Lower sodium intake helps control blood pressure, reduce fluid retention, and improve responsiveness to RAAS medications - all crucial for slowing CKD progression.

Target: <800 mg/day for Stage 3 CKD and beyond Reducing dietary phosphorus (by limiting processed foods and dairy) lowers risk of vascular calcification and secondary hyperparathyroidism. Use phosphate binders with meals as needed in later stages.

steps.dose: 650-1300 mg BID if serum CO₂ <20 mmol/L
steps.why: Alkali therapy corrects metabolic acidosis, which can otherwise accelerate CKD progression and bone loss. The goal is to maintain serum CO₂ >22 mmol/L.

Monitor labs regularly (GFR, potassium, phosphorus, bicarbonate) Encourage a DASH or Mediterranean diet early on; adjust based on labs Collaborate with nephrology and dietetics for personalized care as CKD advances

protocols.title: Nephrolithiasis
protocols.background: Nephrolithiasis, or kidney stones, refers to the formation of solid crystalline aggregates in the renal collecting system, often composed of calcium oxalate, calcium phosphate, uric acid, or cystine. Etiologies include dehydration, hypercalciuria, hyperoxaluria, low urinary citrate, dietary factors, genetic predisposition, and metabolic disorders. It affects about 10% of the population, with higher incidence in men and peak onset between ages 30-50. Pathophysiologically, stones form when urinary solutes become supersaturated and precipitate into crystals, which may grow and obstruct urinary flow. Clinically, nephrolithiasis presents with sudden, severe flank pain radiating to the groin, hematuria, nausea, and urinary urgency or frequency. Differential diagnoses include pyelonephritis, appendicitis, ectopic pregnancy, and abdominal aortic aneurysm. Diagnosis is confirmed via non-contrast CT, renal ultrasound, or urinalysis showing hematuria or crystals. Management includes hydration, pain control (NSAIDs or opioids), and stone-specific treatments such as alpha-blockers (eg, tamsulosin) for passage or lithotripsy for larger stones. Prognosis is generally good with proper treatment, but recurrence is common. Complications may include urinary obstruction, infection, hydronephrosis, or renal damage.

steps.why: Goal: ≥2.5 L urine/day (up to 3 L/day for uric acid or cystine stones) High fluid intake dilutes urinary solutes and reduces crystal formation, lowering recurrence risk for all stone types. Use lemon water or herbal teas to support hydration and citrate levels.

steps.agent: Potassium Citrate (for hypocitraturia and uric acid/cystine stones)
steps.dose: 10-20 mEq BID (max 100 mEq/day); adjust based on labs and urine pH
steps.why: Raises urinary citrate and alkalizes urine, preventing calcium oxalate and uric acid stone formation. Monitor potassium and urine pH to avoid over-alkalinization.

steps.dose: 400-500 mg capsule TID or 30-60 drops tincture TID for 6-8 weeks
steps.why: Demonstrated litholytic (ability to dissolve or break stones) activity, helping to reduce stone size and ease passage. Often used for calcium oxalate and uric acid stone prevention.

steps.dose: 200 mg BID
steps.why: Reduces urinary oxalate production by supporting glyoxylate metabolism, particularly in calcium oxalate stone formers. Safe and well-tolerated as a long-term preventive.

protocols.title: Erectile Dysfunction (ED)
protocols.background: Erectile dysfunction (ED) is the persistent inability to achieve or maintain an erection sufficient for satisfactory sexual performance. Etiologies include vascular disease (eg, atherosclerosis), diabetes mellitus, neurological disorders, hypogonadism, medications (eg, antihypertensives, SSRIs), psychological factors, and lifestyle contributors like smoking and alcohol use. ED affects an estimated 30 million men in the U.S., with prevalence increasing with age, particularly in men over 40. Pathophysiologically, ED results from impaired blood flow, nerve signaling, or hormonal imbalance, often involving endothelial dysfunction and reduced nitric oxide availability. Patients may report reduced rigidity, difficulty maintaining erections, or loss of nocturnal erections. Differential diagnoses include hypogonadism, Peyronie’s disease, depression, and medication-induced sexual dysfunction. Diagnosis involves history, physical exam, and targeted labs (eg, testosterone, glucose, lipids), with further evaluation (eg, nocturnal penile tumescence testing) in select cases. Management includes lifestyle modification, treating underlying conditions, and pharmacotherapy - typically PDE5 inhibitors like sildenafil. Prognosis is favorable with appropriate treatment, though ED may signal underlying cardiovascular disease. Complications include reduced quality of life, relationship stress, and psychological distress.

steps.dose: 3-5 g/day or 2 g extended-release, taken 30-60 minutes before sexual activity.

Duration: Ongoing This anti-inflammatory, antioxidant-rich dietary pattern improves endothelial function and reduces metabolic syndrome risk, both of which are key contributors to ED. Combine this with regular aerobic and resistance training for synergistic benefit.

protocols.title: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH)
protocols.background: Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) is a non-malignant enlargement of the prostate gland, commonly affecting men over 50 due to age-related hormonal changes, particularly increased dihydrotestosterone (DHT) activity. It is the most common cause of lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) in aging men, with prevalence rising from 20% in men aged 40-49 to over 80% in those over 70. BPH results from hyperplasia of prostatic stromal and epithelial cells, leading to urethral compression and bladder outlet obstruction. Clinically, it presents with urinary hesitancy, weak stream, nocturia, frequency, urgency, and incomplete emptying. Differential diagnoses include prostate cancer, urinary tract infection, neurogenic bladder, and urethral stricture. Diagnosis is based on symptom assessment (eg, IPSS score), digital rectal exam, urinalysis, PSA levels, and sometimes ultrasound or urodynamic testing. Management includes lifestyle modifications, alpha-blockers (eg, tamsulosin), 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors (eg, finasteride), and surgical options like TURP if severe. Prognosis is generally good, but complications may include acute urinary retention, recurrent UTIs, bladder stones, and renal impairment if untreated.

steps.dose: 160 mg twice daily for at least 3-6 months
steps.why: Inhibits 5-alpha-reductase, reducing dihydrotestosterone (DHT) levels and improving urinary symptoms. Comparable in efficacy to tamsulosin in mild to moderate BPH.

steps.why: Rich in lignans and omega-3s, flaxseed supports hormone metabolism, reduces PSA levels, and improves lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS).

steps.why: Improve urinary flow (Qmax), symptom score (IPSS), and quality of life by supporting bladder function and reducing inflammation.

steps.dose: Lycopene 15 mg/day + Selenium 100-200 mcg/day
steps.why: Lycopene reduces prostate volume and improves symptom scores; selenium adds antioxidant support and may enhance the effects of saw palmetto and lycopene.

protocols.title: Premenstrual Syndrome (PMS)
protocols.background: Premenstrual syndrome (PMS) refers to a group of physical, emotional, and behavioral symptoms that occur cyclically during the luteal phase of the menstrual cycle and resolve shortly after menstruation begins. The exact etiology is unclear but is believed to involve abnormal responses to normal hormonal fluctuations, particularly involving serotonin and progesterone. PMS affects up to 75% of menstruating women, with moderate-to-severe symptoms in about 20-30%, most commonly in women in their late 20s to early 40s. Pathophysiologically, PMS may involve altered neurotransmitter sensitivity, fluid retention, and hormonal imbalances affecting mood and somatic function. Common symptoms include mood swings, irritability, anxiety, fatigue, bloating, breast tenderness, and headaches. Differential diagnoses include premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD), depression, anxiety disorders, hypothyroidism, and anemia. Diagnosis is clinical, requiring symptom tracking over at least two cycles. Management includes lifestyle modifications, aerobic exercise, calcium (500-1200 mg/day), magnesium, vitamin B6, SSRIs, and hormonal contraceptives. Prognosis is favorable with treatment, though some may progress to PMDD. Complications include impaired daily functioning and reduced quality of life if left unaddressed.

steps.dose: Calcium 500 mg + Magnesium 200 mg + Vitamin D 2000 IU daily ongoing. Reassess after 2-3 cycles.
steps.why: This combination consistently improves both physical (cramps, bloating, breast tenderness) and mood symptoms. Calcium regulates neuromuscular tone, magnesium aids cramp relief and fluid balance, and vitamin D supports hormonal regulation.

steps.dose: 1000-2000 mg EPA/DHA daily for 8 weeks.
steps.why: Omega-3s reduce systemic inflammation, improve mood, and lessen pain, often reducing the need for NSAIDs during the luteal phase of the cycle.

steps.why: 1-2 mL tincture BID during luteal phase or continuously. Begin 14 days before menses and repeat monthly. Cimicifuga modulates estrogen, Viburnum acts as an antispasmodic for uterine cramps, and Hypericum supports mood regulation, especially in cases with emotional symptoms or PMDD tendencies.

1 cup (8 oz) TID as needed during symptomatic day during the luteal phase or acutely Chamomile calms the nervous system, reduces anxiety and irritability, and has mild antispasmodic properties supportive for easing cramping.

protocols.title: Endometriosis
protocols.background: Endometriosis is a chronic gynecological condition characterized by the presence of functional endometrial-like tissue outside the uterine cavity, most commonly on the ovaries, pelvic peritoneum, and fallopian tubes. Its exact etiology is unclear, but proposed mechanisms include retrograde menstruation, coelomic metaplasia, and immune dysfunction. Endometriosis affects approximately 10% of reproductive-aged women and is particularly prevalent in those with infertility or chronic pelvic pain. Pathophysiologically, ectopic endometrial implants respond to hormonal cycles, leading to inflammation, scarring, and adhesions. Clinical presentation includes dysmenorrhea, chronic pelvic pain, dyspareunia, infertility, and sometimes bowel or urinary symptoms. Differential diagnoses include pelvic inflammatory disease, irritable bowel syndrome, ovarian cysts, and fibroids. Diagnosis is suspected clinically and confirmed by laparoscopy with biopsy. Management includes NSAIDs, hormonal therapies (eg, combined oral contraceptives, GnRH agonists), and surgical removal of lesions for pain or fertility preservation. Prognosis varies; while symptoms can often be managed effectively, recurrence is common. Complications may include infertility, adhesions, & significant decreased quality of life.

steps.dose: 10 mg daily at bedtime for 12 weeks
steps.why: Melatonin reduces pelvic pain, suppresses estrogen levels, improves sleep, and may lower oxidative stress. It’s especially useful for endometriosis-associated insomnia and pain control.

steps.dose: Vitamin E 1200 IU + Vitamin C 1000 mg daily for 12 weeks
steps.why: This antioxidant combo has been shown to reduce chronic pelvic pain and inflammation, particularly when taken consistently. It may help decrease the intensity of dysmenorrhea and the need for analgesics.

steps.why: Diosmin is a flavonoid that improves microcirculation and reduces pelvic congestion and inflammation. It has shown efficacy in relieving pain associated with endometriosis.

steps.why: Consume 1 serving of fatty fish (eg. salmon, sardines) or 1-2 tbsp ground flax/chia seeds daily A plant-forward, low-fat, high-fruit/vegetable diet with omega-3s helps modulate systemic inflammation, reduce prostaglandin activity, and ease menstrual cramps and pelvic pain.

protocols.notes: This integrative plan emphasizes reducing systemic inflammation, oxidative stress, and estrogenic load - all central to endometriosis pathology. Lifestyle strategies such as pelvic physical therapy, stress reduction, and avoidance of xenoestrogens are encouraged to further support hormonal balance. Monitor symptom progression. OB- GYN referral may be indicated if fertility concerns or refractory pain arise.

protocols.title: Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS)
protocols.background: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is a common endocrine disorder characterized by chronic anovulation, hyperandrogenism, and polycystic ovaries on ultrasound. The etiology is multifactorial, involving genetic predisposition, insulin resistance, and hormonal imbalances. PCOS affects approximately 6-12% of reproductive-aged women and is a leading cause of infertility. Pathophysiologically, insulin resistance promotes excess ovarian androgen production, disrupting follicular development and ovulation. Clinical features include irregular or absent menses, hirsutism, acne, obesity, and polycystic ovaries. Differential diagnoses include hypothyroidism, hyperprolactinemia, non-classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia, and androgen-secreting tumors. Diagnosis is based on the Rotterdam criteria (two of three: oligo/ anovulation, hyperandrogenism, polycystic ovaries). Management includes lifestyle modification, hormonal contraceptives to regulate menses, and metformin for insulin sensitivity. Prognosis is variable; while symptoms can often be managed, complications include infertility, type 2 diabetes, endometrial hyperplasia, and cardiovascular risk.

steps.dose: 2-4 g/day Myo-inositol + 200-400 mcg folic acid, daily for 3-6 months
steps.why: Myo-inositol improves insulin sensitivity, lowers testosterone, and promotes ovulation, making it especially useful in patients with irregular cycles and fertility concerns. It also enhances oocyte quality and may improve SHBG levels.

steps.why: NAC enhances insulin sensitivity and ovulation, and has shown benefit when combined with ovulation-inducing agents like letrozole. Its antioxidant properties support ovarian health and reduce inflammation.

steps.dose: Calcium 500 mg + Vitamin D 600-1000 IU daily for at least 3 months
steps.why: This combo has been shown to improve menstrual regularity, reduce androgen excess, and support ovulation. It may also help reduce inflammation and improve insulin sensitivity in vitamin D-deficient patients.

Consistency and sustainable lifestyle change are key. Monitor ovulation and cardiometabolic markers over time, and consider adding omega-3s or CoQ10 if fertility, lipid abnormalities, or menstrual irregularities persist.

protocols.title: Allergies
protocols.background: Allergies are hypersensitive immune responses to typically harmless substances (allergens) such as pollen, dust mites, foods, or medications. Etiology involves genetic predisposition and environmental exposures that trigger exaggerated IgE- mediated immune reactions. Allergic conditions are highly prevalent, affecting up to 30% of adults and 40% of children globally, with increasing incidence in industrialized nations. Pathophysiologically, allergens activate mast cells via allergen-specific IgE, leading to histamine and cytokine release that causes inflammation and tissue irritation. Clinical manifestations vary by system and include rhinitis, conjunctivitis, urticaria, eczema, wheezing, or anaphylaxis. Differential diagnoses depend on the organ system and include viral infections, asthma, contact dermatitis, or food intolerances. Diagnosis is based on clinical history, skin prick testing, or specific IgE blood tests. Management includes allergen avoidance, antihistamines, corticosteroids, leukotriene receptor antagonists, and immunotherapy. Prognosis is generally favorable with management, though complications may include chronic sinusitis, asthma, or life-threatening anaphylaxis in severe cases.

steps.dose: Quercetin 500 mg twice daily + Vitamin C 1000 mg twice daily, ongoing during allergy season
steps.why: Quercetin stabilizes mast cells and reduces histamine release, while vitamin C enhances its absorption and independently lowers circulating histamine levels. This combo effectively addresses symptoms of sneezing, itching, and congestion.

300 mg daily freeze-dried leaf for 8 weeks Nettle has antihistamine and anti-inflammatory effects, making it ideal for acute seasonal allergy relief. It can be used alongside conventional antihistamines or other natural therapies.

steps.dose: 3000 mg daily (divided into 2 doses) for 4 weeks
steps.why: MSM reduces nasal congestion, itching, and rhinorrhea, as shown in clinical trials. It supports mucosal integrity and reduces oxidative stress associated with allergic responses.

steps.dose: 5-10 billion CFU/day for at least 8 weeks
steps.why: Probiotics help regulate immune function, reduce Th2-skewed allergic responses, and improve nasal and ocular symptoms. Choose a well-researched multi-strain formula with proven respiratory tract benefits.

protocols.notes: This plan addresses both acute symptom relief and long-term immune modulation. Combine targeted supplements with dietary flavonoids, vitamin C-rich foods, and environmental control measures (eg. HEPA filters, bedding hygiene). Consider evaluating food sensitivities or oral allergy syndrome in persistent or atypical cases. Regular use of these interventions can significantly improve symptom control and reduce reliance on antihistamines.

protocols.title: Upper Respiratory Infections
protocols.background: Upper respiratory infections (URIs) are acute infections involving the nose, sinuses, pharynx, or larynx, commonly referred to as the common cold. They are most often caused by viruses such as rhinovirus, coronavirus, adenovirus, or respiratory syncytial virus. URIs are highly prevalent worldwide, especially in children who may experience 6-8 episodes annually, and are a leading cause of missed work and school days. Pathophysiologically, viral invasion of the respiratory mucosa triggers local inflammation, mucus production, and immune activation. Symptoms typically include nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, sore throat, cough, low-grade fever, and malaise. Differential diagnoses include allergic rhinitis, influenza, streptococcal pharyngitis, and sinusitis. Diagnosis is clinical, based on symptom pattern and duration. Management is supportive, including rest, hydration, saline nasal irrigation, and over-the-counter analgesics or decongestants. Antibiotics are not indicated unless bacterial superinfection is suspected. Prognosis is excellent, with most cases resolving within 7-10 days. Complications are rare but may include secondary bacterial sinusitis, otitis media, or bronchitis.

steps.dose: Zinc gluconate 25mg TID starting within 24 hours of symptom onset for up to 5 days
steps.why: Zinc supports antiviral immunity and may reduce URI duration by inhibiting viral replication in the oropharynx. Lozenges are most effective when started early and used consistently.

steps.why: Vitamin C has mild antiviral and antioxidant properties and can modestly reduce the duration and severity of URIs, especially in individuals under physical or oxidative stress.

steps.why: These botanicals soothe irritated mucosa, relieve sore throat, and reduce cough. Honey also provides antimicrobial and cough-suppressing benefits.

Encourage rest, hydration, and early initiation of zinc and vitamin C for best results. protocols.title: Osteoarthritis (OA)
protocols.background: Osteoarthritis (OA) is a chronic, degenerative joint disease characterized by progressive loss of articular cartilage, subchondral bone remodeling, and osteophyte formation. It is primarily caused by mechanical wear and tear, but risk factors include aging, joint overuse, obesity, previous injury, and genetic predisposition. OA is the most common form of arthritis, affecting over 32 million adults in the United States, particularly those over 50. Pathophysiologically, cartilage breakdown leads to joint space narrowing, inflammation, and bony changes that cause pain and reduced mobility. Clinically, OA presents with joint pain worsened by activity and relieved by rest, morning stiffness lasting less than 30 minutes, crepitus, and limited range of motion - commonly affecting knees, hips, hands, and spine. Differential diagnoses include rheumatoid arthritis, gout, bursitis, and referred pain. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by imaging (X-ray showing joint space narrowing, osteophytes) and exclusion of inflammatory markers. Management includes weight loss, physical therapy, NSAIDs, intra-articular corticosteroids, and joint replacement in advanced cases. Prognosis is variable; while OA is non-fatal, it can lead to significant disability. Complications include chronic pain, reduced quality of life, and loss of joint function.

steps.dose: Glucosamine sulfate 1500 mg + Chondroitin sulfate 1200 mg + MSM 1000 mg daily for 12 weeks
steps.why: This combination supports cartilage integrity, reduces joint stiffness, and has mild to moderate pain-relieving effects. MSM adds anti-inflammatory synergy and is generally well-tolerated.

Adopt Mediterranean dietary pattern and consume ~12 cherries or 4 oz tart cherry juice (low sugar) daily This diet reduces systemic inflammation and metabolic burden on joints, while cherries may lower CRP and joint pain via antioxidant and anti-inflammatory polyphenols.

steps.dose: 500 mg BID on an empty stomach for 2 weeks
steps.why: Bromelain is a proteolytic enzyme with fast-acting anti-inflammatory and analgesic properties, making it useful for acute OA flares or as an NSAID alternative.

steps.dose: 150+ minutes/week of low-impact movement (eg. swimming, cycling, walking)
steps.why: Aim for 5-10% weight loss over 6-12 months Exercise improves joint mobility and function, while even modest weight loss significantly reduces pain and inflammatory markers in overweight individuals with OA.

protocols.notes: This integrative plan addresses OA from multiple angles - structural support, inflammation, metabolism, and physical function. Dietary changes and movement are foundational, while evidence-based supplements like glucosamine, MSM, and bromelain enhance symptom relief. Reinforce that consistent, joint-friendly activity and long-term weight loss are central to slowing OA progression.

protocols.title: Gout
protocols.background: Gout is a form of inflammatory arthritis caused by monosodium urate crystal deposition in joints due to chronic hyperuricemia. Etiologies include genetic predisposition, high purine intake (eg, red meat, alcohol), obesity, renal insufficiency, and medications such as diuretics. Gout affects about 4% of U.S. adults, with higher prevalence in men and postmenopausal women. Pathophysiologically, excess serum uric acid leads to crystal precipitation in joints, triggering intense neutrophilic inflammation. It classically presents as sudden, severe pain, redness, and swelling in a single joint - most commonly the first metatarsophalangeal joint (podagra). Differential diagnoses include septic arthritis, pseudogout, cellulitis, and rheumatoid arthritis. Diagnosis is confirmed by joint aspiration showing negatively birefringent urate crystals; serum uric acid levels and imaging may support the diagnosis. Management includes NSAIDs, colchicine, or corticosteroids for acute flares, and urate-lowering therapy (eg, allopurinol) for long-term prevention. Prognosis is good with adherence to therapy, but complications include tophi, joint destruction, and chronic arthritis if poorly managed.

steps.dose: Drink 2-3 liters of water daily + consume 10-12 cherries daily
steps.why: Adequate hydration enhances renal excretion of uric acid, while cherries reduce serum uric acid and flare frequency through anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effects.

steps.dose: Quercetin 500 mg/day + Vitamin C 500 mg/day for ongoing support
steps.why: Quercetin inhibits xanthine oxidase, lowering uric acid production, while vitamin C modestly enhances uric acid excretion. Both are also present in cherries and support flare prevention.

Adopt a DASH-style diet emphasizing vegetables, legumes, low-fat dairy, and whole grains. Avoid consuming organ meats, beer, and high-fructose foods. This dietary pattern directly addresses both triggers and contributors to gout flares.

Aim for 5% body weight loss over 3-6 months through whole-food eating and low-impact exercise. Weight reduction helps to significantly lower uric acid, thereby reducing the frequency of gout attacks, especially in metabolically active individuals.

protocols.notes: This plan targets gout from both preventative and symptomatic angles by reducing uric acid production and enhancing excretion. Cherries, hydration, and quercetin offer natural alternatives to pharmacologic urate-lowering therapy, especially in early or mild cases. Emphasize gradual dietary shifts and flare prevention education for long-term success.

protocols.title: Osteoporosis
protocols.background: Osteoporosis is a skeletal disorder characterized by reduced bone mass and microarchitectural deterioration, leading to increased bone fragility and fracture risk. It most commonly results from aging, estrogen deficiency (especially postmenopause), chronic glucocorticoid use, or nutritional deficiencies in calcium and vitamin D. Osteoporosis affects over 10 million people in the U.S., with higher prevalence in postmenopausal women and older adults. Pathophysiologically, an imbalance between bone resorption and formation leads to porous, weakened bone. Osteoporosis is often asymptomatic until a fracture occurs, typically in the hip, vertebrae, or wrist. Differential diagnoses include osteomalacia, multiple myeloma, and metastatic bone disease. Diagnosis is made via dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) scan showing a T-score ≤ -2.5. Management includes weight-bearing exercise, calcium (1000-1200 mg/day), vitamin D (800-1000 IU/day), bisphosphonates, and fall prevention strategies. Prognosis is favorable with early intervention, but complications such as fragility fractures, chronic pain, loss of independence, and increased mortality (especially with hip fractures) are significant concerns.

steps.dose: Calcium 500 mg + Magnesium 400 mg + Vitamin D3 1000 IU + Vitamin K2 200 mcg daily
steps.why: This foundational combo supports bone mineralization, calcium absorption, and regulation of calcium into the bone matrix. K2 specifically activates osteocalcin, directing calcium into bone and away from arteries.

steps.dose: Walk 30 minutes at least 5x/week + resistance training 2-3x/week
steps.why: Mechanical loading stimulates osteoblast activity and improves bone density, while resistance and balance training reduce fracture risk by improving muscle strength and fall prevention.

Emphasize yogurt, leafy greens, legumes, nuts, soy foods, olive oil, and fish. Limit alcohol to 1-2 drinks daily. This pattern provides key nutrients like calcium, magnesium, protein, and phytoestrogens (from soy), supporting bone mineral density (BMD) and reducing inflammation-related bone loss.

steps.why: Strontium mimics calcium in bone and may enhance bone formation while reducing resorption. It has shown promising results in improving BMD when used adjunctively.

protocols.notes: This plan integrates diet, movement, and supplementation to address the multifactorial nature of osteoporosis. Prioritize food-based calcium and magnesium, and use a targeted supplement when needed. Encourage lifelong weight-bearing movement, especially in postmenopausal women. Monitor BMD periodically, and reinforce the importance of fall prevention strategies to preserve independence as well as overall quality of life.

protocols.title: Attention Deficit Disorder
protocols.background: Attention Deficit Disorder (ADD), now classified under Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), predominantly inattentive presentation, is a neurodevelopmental disorder marked by persistent patterns of inattention that interfere with daily functioning. Etiology is multifactorial, involving genetic predisposition, neurochemical imbalances (especially dopamine and norepinephrine), and environmental factors such as prenatal exposures or early adversity. ADHD affects about 5-10% of children and 2-5% of adults, with ADD more common in females and often underdiagnosed due to its less overt hyperactivity. Pathophysiologically, dysregulation in fronto-striatal circuits and neurotransmitter signaling impairs executive functioning and attention regulation. Clinical features include distractibility, forgetfulness, disorganization, poor task follow-through, and difficulty sustaining attention, often emerging before age 12. Differential diagnoses include anxiety, depression, learning disorders, and thyroid dysfunction. Diagnosis is clinical, based on DSM-5 criteria, corroborated by behavioral scales and input from multiple settings (eg, school, home). Management includes behavioral therapy, academic accommodations, and pharmacologic treatment - typically stimulants like methylphenidate or non-stimulants such as atomoxetine. Prognosis is variable; many symptoms improve with age, but untreated can lead to academic underachievement, low self-esteem, and functional impairments.

steps.dose: EPA dominant omega-3 fatty acid 3 grams daily for 12 weeks
steps.why: EPA-rich omega-3s support cognitive function, reduce inattention, and modulate dopamine transmission. Algae-based EPA is a good vegetarian option and shows mild but consistent benefit in symptom reduction.

steps.dose: Zinc 15 mg twice daily + Magnesium 200 mg daily for 12 weeks
steps.why: Zinc enhances the effectiveness of stimulant medications and supports neurotransmitter activity, while magnesium contributes to neurological stability and may reduce restlessness and irritability symptoms.

Remove artificial additives and trial elimination of common triggers (dairy, wheat, soy) for 4 weeks. Removing synthetic dyes and preservatives can reduce hyperactivity in sensitive individuals. Elimination diets may identify food sensitivities that contribute to attention or behavior issues - reintroduce foods one at a time to monitor response.

steps.dose: Vitamin D 2000 IU/day for 3 months
steps.why: Vitamin D plays a role in brain development and has shown small but meaningful benefits when used in combination with stimulant medications. Deficiency is common and easy to address with safe daily dosing.

protocols.notes: This integrative plan supports attention and behavior by targeting nutrient deficiencies, inflammatory dietary triggers, and neurocognitive support. Avoid artificial additives, support a whole-food diet, and consider gentle lifestyle strategies like regular outdoor time and reducing toxin exposure (lead, tobacco). Individual responses vary - consistent observation and support are key. Always collaborate with mental health professionals for diagnosis and medication guidance.

protocols.title: Migraine
protocols.background: Migraine is a chronic neurological disorder characterized by recurrent moderate to severe headaches, often unilateral and pulsating, typically lasting 4-72 hours and associated with nausea, photophobia, and phonophobia. Etiology involves genetic predisposition and environmental triggers such as stress, hormonal fluctuations, certain foods, and sleep disturbances. Migraine affects approximately 12% of the global population, with higher prevalence in women, especially during reproductive years. Pathophysiologically, migraines involve cortical spreading depression, trigeminovascular system activation, and neuroinflammation, leading to the release of vasoactive peptides like CGRP. Clinical presentation may include a prodrome, aura (in about 25% of patients), the headache phase, and postdrome. Differential diagnoses include tension-type headache, cluster headache, sinusitis, and intracranial pathology. Diagnosis is clinical, based on the International Classification of Headache Disorders criteria. Management includes trigger avoidance, lifestyle modification, acute treatments (eg, NSAIDs, triptans), and preventive therapies (eg, beta-blockers, topiramate, CGRP antagonists). Prognosis varies; many experience episodic migraines manageable with treatment, but some progress to chronic migraine. Complications may include reduced quality of life as well as comorbid anxiety and/or depression.

steps.dose: Riboflavin 400 mg + Magnesium 600 mg + CoQ10 150 mg daily for prevention for 3 months
steps.why: This trio supports mitochondrial function, reduces neuronal excitability, and lowers migraine frequency and severity. These nutrients are among the most evidence-supported for migraine prevention.

steps.why: Ginger acts as an anti-inflammatory and anti-nausea agent, offering safe and effective acute migraine relief.

steps.dose: 3 mg daily at bedtime for ongoing preventative support
steps.why: Melatonin helps regulate circadian rhythms and supports sleep quality, which can reduce migraine frequency, especially among individuals with insomnia or irregular sleep patterns.

Emphasize an anti-inflammatory whole foods diet. Avoid skipping meals. Avoid known personal triggers. Eating meals consistently and emphasizing nutrient-dense foods help stabilize blood sugar and reduce inflammation. Identifying and eliminating triggers (especially common dietary triggers including wine, chocolate, aged cheese, artificial sweeteners) can significantly reduce migraine attack frequency and severity.

protocols.notes: This plan combines prevention and acute care through nutrient therapy, botanicals, and lifestyle changes. Begin with targeted daily supplements and encourage patients to track symptoms and triggers with a migraine diary. Address sleep, stress, and diet patterns alongside natural therapies for optimal long-term success. Consider referring for advanced care if migraines become chronic or disabling.

protocols.title: Seizures
protocols.background: A seizure is a transient episode of abnormal, excessive, or synchronous neuronal activity in the brain, leading to changes in behavior, sensation, movement, or consciousness. Etiologies include epilepsy, head trauma, stroke, brain tumors, infections, metabolic disturbances (eg, hypoglycemia, hyponatremia), and drug or alcohol withdrawal. Seizures affect about 8-10% of people at some point in life, with epilepsy diagnosed when two or more unprovoked seizures occur. Pathophysiologically, seizures result from an imbalance between excitatory and inhibitory neural signals, often involving glutamate and GABA pathways. Clinical presentation varies by type: generalized seizures may involve tonic-clonic movements and loss of consciousness, while focal seizures can present with localized motor activity, sensory changes, or altered awareness. Differential diagnoses include syncope, transient ischemic attack, migraine, and psychogenic non- epileptic seizures. Diagnosis is based on clinical history, EEG, and neuroimaging to identify underlying causes. Management includes treating the underlying cause, antiepileptic drugs (eg, levetiracetam, valproate), and lifestyle modifications to reduce triggers. Prognosis depends on the cause and seizure control; while many achieve good control with medication, complications can include status epilepticus, injury during seizures, and psychosocial impacts.

steps.why: Adopt a classic ketogenic diet consisting of about 89% fat, 8% protein, 3% carbs Initiate this under clinical supervision with multivitamin, calcium, vitamin D, and trace mineral support. The ketogenic diet alters brain energy metabolism and increases GABA, thereby reducing seizure frequency, especially effective in intractable epilepsy. Monitor for nutrient deficiencies and potential side effects.

steps.dose: Vitamin D3 2000 IU/day (adjust dose based on labs) + Magnesium glycinate 400 mg/day ongoing
steps.why: Vitamin D repletion supports neurologic function and may reduce seizure frequency in deficient individuals. Magnesium is essential for membrane stability and neuronal excitability, especially on keto diets.

steps.dose: 500 mg/day of L-carnitine for those on valproic acid taken ongoing as needed
steps.why: Valproate depletes carnitine, contributing to fatigue and potential hepatotoxicity. Supplementing carnitine can reduce side effects and support mitochondrial function.

steps.dose: 400-800 IU/day of mixed tocopherols for 3 months
steps.why: Vitamin E acts as an antioxidant and may reduce seizure frequency by decreasing oxidative stress in the brain, particularly in patients presenting with idiopathic or medication-resistant epilepsy.

protocols.notes: This integrative plan supports neurologic stability through diet, targeted nutrients, and coordination with medical care. The ketogenic diet remains the most evidence-based non-pharmaceutical option for refractory epilepsy. Supplementation should be personalized and carefully monitored, particularly when anticonvulsants are used. Always collaborate with neurology before initiating significant dietary or supplement changes.

protocols.title: Multiple Sclerosis
protocols.background: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic autoimmune demyelinating disease of the central nervous system characterized by recurrent episodes of neurologic dysfunction due to immune-mediated destruction of myelin and axons. The exact etiology is unknown but involves a combination of genetic susceptibility and environmental triggers, such as Epstein-Barr virus and low vitamin D levels. MS affects about 2.8 million people worldwide, with higher prevalence in women and individuals of northern European descent, typically presenting between ages 20-40. Pathophysiologically, autoreactive lymphocytes cross the blood-brain barrier, leading to demyelination, inflammation, and eventual neurodegeneration. Clinical presentation varies but may include optic neuritis, limb weakness, sensory disturbances, ataxia, bladder dysfunction, and fatigue. The disease may follow a relapsing-remitting, secondary progressive, or primary progressive course. Differential diagnoses include neuromyelitis optica, lupus, B12 deficiency, and stroke. Diagnosis relies on clinical features, MRI showing demyelinating lesions, and CSF analysis with oligoclonal bands. Management includes acute relapse treatment with corticosteroids, disease-modifying therapies (eg, interferons, monoclonal antibodies), and symptomatic support. Prognosis varies, with most patients experiencing gradual decline over decades. Complications include mobility loss, cognitive impairment, depression, and reduced quality of life.

steps.dose: 2000 IU/day (adjust as necessary to maintain ~45 ng/mL serum level)
steps.why: Vitamin D modulates immune function, reduces pro-inflammatory cytokines, and may lower relapse rates. Deficiency is strongly linked to increased disease activity and disability progression.

steps.dose: 2 grams omega-3 (combined EPA + DHA) taken daily for 6 months

protocols.title: Parkinson’S
protocols.background: Parkinson’s disease is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by motor and non-motor symptoms resulting from the loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra of the basal ganglia. Its etiology is multifactorial, involving genetic mutations (eg, LRRK2, P ARK7) and environmental exposures (eg, pesticides, heavy metals). It affects approximately 1% of individuals over age 60, with higher prevalence in men. Pathophysiologically, dopamine deficiency disrupts the regulation of movement and leads to the hallmark motor symptoms: resting tremor, bradykinesia, rigidity, and postural instability. Non-motor features include constipation, anosmia, depression, cognitive decline, and sleep disturbances. Differential diagnoses include essential tremor, multiple system atrophy, progressive supranuclear palsy, and drug-induced parkinsonism. Diagnosis is clinical, based on history and neurologic exam, with supportive imaging like DaTscan if needed. Management includes dopaminergic therapies (eg, levodopa/carbidopa), MAO-B inhibitors, physical therapy, and deep brain stimulation in advanced cases. Prognosis is variable; although not fatal, Parkinson’s leads to progressive disability. Complications include falls, aspiration pneumonia, dementia, and loss of independence.

Nutritional strategies should complement (but not replace) conventional treatment, in close coordination with neurology.

protocols.title: Alzheimer’S
protocols.background: Alzheimer’s disease is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder and the most common cause of dementia, characterized by gradual cognitive decline affecting memory, language, and executive function. The etiology is multifactorial, involving genetic factors (eg, APOE ε4 allele), age-related neuronal changes, and environmental influences. Alzheimer’s affects over 6 million Americans, primarily those over 65, with risk increasing with age. Pathophysiologically, the disease is marked by accumulation of beta-amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles composed of hyperphosphorylated tau protein, leading to synaptic dysfunction and neuronal loss, especially in the hippocampus and cortex. Clinically, it presents with progressive memory loss, difficulty with language, impaired judgment, and later, behavioral changes and loss of daily functioning. Differential diagnoses include vascular dementia, Lewy body dementia, frontotemporal dementia, and depression. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by cognitive testing (eg, MMSE, MoCA), MRI, and sometimes PET imaging or CSF biomarkers. Management focuses on symptom control and slowing progression using cholinesterase inhibitors (eg, donepezil) and NMDA receptor antagonists (eg, memantine), along with supportive care. Prognosis is poor, with average survival of 4-8 years after diagnosis. Complications include complete dependence, malnutrition, infections, and death, often from aspiration pneumonia.

protocols.title: Diabetes Mellitus (T2DM)
protocols.background: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) is a chronic metabolic disorder characterized by insulin resistance and relative insulin deficiency, leading to hyperglycemia. Etiology involves genetic predisposition and lifestyle factors such as obesity, physical inactivity, and poor diet. T2DM accounts for over 90% of diabetes cases worldwide and is increasingly prevalent in both adults and adolescents, particularly in populations with higher rates of obesity and metabolic syndrome. Pathophysiologically, insulin resistance in muscle and liver tissues, combined with impaired pancreatic beta-cell function, disrupts glucose homeostasis. Clinical presentation may be insidious, with symptoms including polyuria, polydipsia, fatigue, blurred vision, and recurrent infections, though many cases are diagnosed incidentally. Differential diagnoses include type 1 diabetes, latent autoimmune diabetes in adults (LADA), and medication-induced hyperglycemia. Diagnosis is confirmed by elevated fasting glucose (≥126 mg/dL), HbA1c (≥6.5%), or 2-hour OGTT. Management includes lifestyle modifications, metformin as first-line pharmacotherapy, and additional agents (eg, GLP-1 agonists, SGLT2 inhibitors) as needed. Prognosis improves with glycemic control, but long-term complications can include cardiovascular disease, nephropathy, neuropathy, and retinopathy. protocols.title: Coronary Artery Disease
protocols.background: Coronary artery disease (CAD) is a condition characterized by the narrowing or blockage of coronary arteries due to atherosclerosis, leading to reduced blood flow to the myocardium. Etiology involves modifiable risk factors such as hypertension, hyperlipidemia, smoking, diabetes, and sedentary lifestyle, as well as non-modifiable factors like age, male sex, and family history. CAD is the leading cause of death globally, particularly prevalent in individuals over 45 and those with metabolic syndrome. Pathophysiologically, endothelial injury triggers lipid accumulation, inflammation, and plaque formation in coronary vessels, which can rupture and cause thrombosis. Clinically, CAD presents with exertional chest pain (angina), dyspnea, or may be silent, especially in diabetics. Acute presentations include unstable angina or myocardial infarction. Differential diagnoses include aortic dissection, pericarditis, GERD, and pulmonary embolism. Diagnosis is made via ECG, stress testing, cardiac biomarkers, and coronary angiography. Management includes lifestyle changes, antiplatelet agents (aspirin), statins, beta-blockers, nitrates, and revascularization (PCI or CABG) when indicated. Prognosis varies with disease severity and treatment adherence; complications include heart failure, arrhythmias, myocardial infarction, and sudden cardiac death.

protocols.title: Hypertension
protocols.background: Hypertension is defined as persistently elevated blood pressure, typically ≥130/80 mmHg, and is classified as either primary (essential) or secondary to underlying conditions such as renal disease, endocrine disorders, or medication use. Primary hypertension accounts for about 90-95% of cases and arises from a combination of genetic predisposition, high salt intake, obesity, stress, and sedentary lifestyle. It affects nearly half of adults in the United States and is a major risk factor for cardiovascular morbidity and mortality. Pathophysiologically, hypertension involves increased systemic vascular resistance due to dysregulation of vascular tone, the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, and sympathetic nervous system overactivity. Most patients are asymptomatic, but severe or prolonged hypertension may present with headaches, visual changes, or signs of end-organ damage. Differential diagnoses include white-coat hypertension, anxiety, and secondary causes like hyperaldosteronism or pheochromocytoma. Diagnosis requires consistent blood pressure measurements, often supplemented by ambulatory monitoring. Management focuses on lifestyle modifications (dietary sodium restriction, weight loss, exercise) and pharmacologic therapy (thiazide diuretics, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, calcium channel blockers). Prognosis is good with treatment but uncontrolled hypertension can lead to complications such as stroke, myocardial infarction, chronic kidney disease, and heart failure. protocols.title: Atrial Fibrillation
protocols.background: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most common sustained cardiac arrhythmia, characterized by disorganized, rapid electrical impulses in the atria leading to ineffective atrial contractions and an irregularly irregular ventricular rhythm. Etiologies include hypertension, coronary artery disease, valvular heart disease, heart failure, hyperthyroidism, alcohol use, and aging. AF affects over 6 million adults in the U.S., with increasing prevalence in individuals over age 65 and those with cardiovascular comorbidities. Pathophysiologically, structural and electrical remodeling of atrial tissue promotes ectopic foci and reentrant circuits, especially near the pulmonary veins. Clinical presentation may include palpitations, fatigue, dyspnea, dizziness, or it may be asymptomatic. Differential diagnoses include other supraventricular tachycardias, premature atrial contractions, and sinus arrhythmia. Diagnosis is confirmed via ECG showing absent P waves and irregularly irregular QRS complexes. Management includes rate or rhythm control (beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, antiarrhythmics), stroke prevention with anticoagulation (based on CHA₂DS₂-V ASc score), and procedures like cardioversion or catheter ablation when indicated. Prognosis depends on underlying disease and stroke risk; complications include thromboembolism (notably stroke), heart failure, and reduced quality of life.

protocols.title: Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease
protocols.background: Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) is a chronic condition in which stomach contents flow backward into the esophagus, causing symptoms or mucosal injury due to impaired lower esophageal sphincter (LES) function. Etiologies include LES dysfunction, hiatal hernia, obesity, pregnancy, smoking, and certain foods or medications that reduce LES tone. GERD affects up to 20% of adults in Western countries and is a leading cause of outpatient visits for gastrointestinal complaints. Pathophysiologically, refluxed gastric acid and bile irritate the esophageal lining, leading to inflammation and symptoms. Clinically, GERD presents with heartburn, regurgitation, chest discomfort, and sometimes chronic cough, hoarseness, or dysphagia. Differential diagnoses include peptic ulcer disease, esophagitis, angina, and esophageal motility disorders. Diagnosis is often clinical but may be confirmed with upper endoscopy, pH monitoring, or esophageal manometry when atypical or refractory. Management includes lifestyle modifications (eg, weight loss, avoiding triggers, head-of-bed elevation), acid suppression with proton pump inhibitors (PPIs), and surgical options (eg, fundoplication) in select cases. Prognosis is favorable with treatment, but complications can include erosive esophagitis, strictures, Barrett’s esophagus, and increased risk of esophageal adenocarcinoma.

Adopt a Mediterranean-style low-glycemic diet on an ongoing basis. This eating pattern reduces reflux by minimizing gastric distention and improving gastric emptying. Evidence supports the Mediterranean diet being as effective as PPIs in symptom control and improves overall GI health.

Identify and avoid symptom-specific triggers using a food/symptom diary over a 4 week elimination phase. Common triggers include peppermint, citrus, chocolate, tomatoes, fried foods, alcohol, and caffeine.

protocols.title: Hepatic Steatosis
protocols.background: Hepatic steatosis, also known as fatty liver disease, is characterized by excessive fat accumulation in hepatocytes, typically exceeding 5% of liver weight. It can be classified as nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) or alcoholic fatty liver disease (AFLD), depending on alcohol consumption history. Etiologies include obesity, insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes, dyslipidemia, and excessive alcohol use. NAFLD is the most common liver disorder in industrialized nations, affecting up to 25% of adults globally. Pathophysiologically, hepatic steatosis arises from imbalances in lipid uptake, synthesis, oxidation, and export, often driven by insulin resistance and oxidative stress. Most patients are asymptomatic, though some may report fatigue or right upper quadrant discomfort. Differential diagnoses include viral hepatitis, autoimmune hepatitis, hemochromatosis, and drug-induced liver injury. Diagnosis is typically made via imaging (eg, ultrasound, CT, MRI) and supported by liver function tests; biopsy is reserved for suspected steatohepatitis. Management focuses on lifestyle interventions - weight loss, diet, exercise - and control of metabolic comorbidities. Prognosis is generally good in simple steatosis, but progression to nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH), fibrosis, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma is possible if risk factors persist.

protocols.title: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease
protocols.background: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is a progressive respiratory condition characterized by persistent airflow limitation due to chronic bronchitis, emphysema, or both. The primary etiology is long-term exposure to noxious particles, most commonly cigarette smoke, though environmental pollutants, occupational exposures, and genetic factors (eg, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency) also contribute. COPD affects over 16 million adults in the U.S. and is a leading cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide, especially in individuals over age 40 with a smoking history. Pathophysiologically, COPD involves chronic airway inflammation, mucous hypersecretion, and alveolar wall destruction, leading to decreased elastic recoil and airflow obstruction. Clinical presentation includes chronic cough, sputum production, progressive dyspnea, and wheezing, often worsening over time. Differential diagnoses include asthma, heart failure, bronchiectasis, and interstitial lung disease. Diagnosis is confirmed with spirometry showing a post-bronchodilator FEV₁/FVC ratio <0.70. Management includes smoking cessation, bronchodilators (eg, LABAs, LAMAs), inhaled corticosteroids in select cases, pulmonary rehabilitation, and oxygen therapy for advanced disease. Prognosis varies with severity but is generally progressive; complications include respiratory infections, pulmonary hypertension, acute exacerbations, and respiratory failure.

protocols.title: Lower Respiratory Infection
protocols.background: Lower respiratory infections (LRIs) involve the trachea, bronchi, bronchioles, and lungs, with pneumonia and bronchitis being the most common forms. Etiologies include viral pathogens (eg, influenza, RSV , SARS-CoV-2), bacterial agents (eg, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae), and less commonly fungi or atypical organisms. LRIs are a leading cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide, particularly affecting children under five, older adults, and immunocompromised individuals. Pathophysiologically, pathogens invade the lower airways, triggering inflammation, mucus production, and impaired gas exchange. Clinically, LRIs present with cough, sputum production, fever, dyspnea, and chest pain; pneumonia may additionally cause rales, decreased breath sounds, or hypoxia. Differential diagnoses include asthma, COPD exacerbation, pulmonary embolism, and heart failure. Diagnosis is based on clinical findings, chest imaging (especially for pneumonia), and supportive lab tests like CBC or sputum culture. Management depends on the cause and severity - viral infections may be self-limited or require antivirals, while bacterial infections are treated with appropriate antibiotics. Prognosis is generally good with prompt treatment but worsens with age, comorbidities, or delayed care. Complications: respiratory failure, sepsis, pleural effusion, and lung abscess.

protocols.title: Irritable Bowel Disease
protocols.background: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is a chronic, relapsing-remitting inflammatory disorder of the gastrointestinal tract, primarily Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis. While the exact etiology is unknown, it is thought to result from a dysregulated immune response to intestinal microbiota in genetically susceptible individuals, influenced by environmental factors such as diet, smoking, and antibiotic use. IBD affects over 3 million people in the U.S., with peak onset between ages 15-35. Pathophysiologically, Crohn’s disease can affect any part of the GI tract with transmural inflammation and skip lesions, whereas ulcerative colitis involves continuous superficial inflammation limited to the colon and rectum. Common symptoms include abdominal pain, diarrhea (often bloody in UC), weight loss, fatigue, and extraintestinal manifestations like arthritis or skin rashes. Differential diagnoses include irritable bowel syndrome, celiac disease, infections, and colorectal cancer. Diagnosis is based on clinical history, endoscopy with biopsy, imaging, and inflammatory markers (eg, CRP, fecal calprotectin). Management includes anti-inflammatory agents (5-ASA), immunosuppressants, biologics (eg, TNF inhibitors), dietary support, and sometimes surgery. Prognosis varies; while many achieve remission, complications may include strictures, fistulas, abscesses, malnutrition, and increased colorectal cancer risk, especially in longstanding ulcerative colitis.

protocols.title: Celiac Disease
protocols.background: Celiac disease is a chronic autoimmune disorder triggered by the ingestion of gluten - a protein found in wheat, barley, and rye - in genetically susceptible individuals, leading to small intestinal inflammation and villous atrophy. The condition is strongly associated with HLA-DQ2 and HLA-DQ8 genotypes. It affects about 1% of the global population, though many cases remain undiagnosed due to variable symptom presentation. Pathophysiologically, gluten exposure in affected individuals activates T cells, leading to mucosal damage in the small intestine and impaired nutrient absorption. Clinical presentation ranges from classic symptoms like chronic diarrhea, weight loss, bloating, and fatigue to non-GI manifestations such as anemia, dermatitis herpetiformis, osteoporosis, or infertility. Differential diagnoses include irritable bowel syndrome, inflammatory bowel disease, lactose intolerance, and small intestinal bacterial overgrowth. Diagnosis is based on positive serologic tests (eg, anti-tTG IgA), confirmed by duodenal biopsy showing villous atrophy. Management requires strict lifelong adherence to a gluten-free diet, which typically leads to symptom resolution and mucosal healing. Prognosis is excellent with dietary compliance, but complications of untreated disease include malnutrition, osteoporosis, infertility, and increased risk of intestinal lymphoma.

Eliminating gluten halts autoimmune destruction of the small intestine and allows mucosal healing. Use certified gluten-free substitutes such as quinoa, rice, buckwheat, corn, and GF oats. Cross-contamination must be meticulously avoided, including during food prep and dining out, to ensure full symptom resolution and prevent long-term complications.

This helps balance blood sugar, reduce inflammation, and support gut healing, while avoiding the common pitfall of processed GF diets that can worsen metabolic health and nutrient density.

protocols.notes: Managing celiac disease requires strict, lifelong dietary vigilance supported by targeted nutrient repletion and whole-food choices. Persistent symptoms despite adherence should prompt reevaluation for cross- contamination, coexisting intolerances, or microscopic colitis. Regular lab monitoring ensures recovery and helps detect deficiencies or complications early. Educate patients on label reading, gluten cross-contact, and meal planning to promote long-term success.

protocols.title: Irritable Bowel Syndrome
protocols.background: Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is a functional gastrointestinal disorder characterized by chronic abdominal pain and altered bowel habits (diarrhea, constipation, or both) in the absence of identifiable structural or biochemical abnormalities. The etiology is multifactorial, involving altered gut-brain axis communication, visceral hypersensitivity, dysbiosis, and psychosocial stressors. IBS affects 10-15% of the global population, with a higher prevalence in women and individuals under 50. Pathophysiologically, IBS involves abnormal gastrointestinal motility, heightened pain perception, and often post-infectious or inflammatory changes in the gut. Clinical presentation includes recurrent abdominal pain associated with changes in stool frequency or form, bloating, and relief after defecation. Differential diagnoses include inflammatory bowel disease, celiac disease, lactose intolerance, and colorectal cancer. Diagnosis is clinical, based on Rome IV criteria, and supported by exclusion of red flags (eg, weight loss, anemia, GI bleeding). Management includes dietary modifications (eg, low FODMAP diet), fiber, antispasmodics, psychological therapies, and medications targeting predominant symptoms (eg, laxatives or antidiarrheals). Prognosis is generally good, with symptom control achievable in most patients, but quality of life may be significantly impacted. IBS does not increase the risk of colorectal cancer or inflammatory complications.

steps.why: Eliminate high-FODMAP foods for 4 weeks, then gradually reintroduce under supervision. Reduces fermentation and gas production in the gut, improving bloating, pain, and stool irregularities. Intended as a short-term intervention to help identify triggers and restore digestive tolerance.

steps.dose: 10 grams daily for 8 weeks.
steps.why: Incorporating soluble fiber improves stool form and regularity, especially in IBS with constipation (IBS-C), by normalizing transit time and feeding beneficial gut bacteria. Better tolerated than insoluble fibers and effective across different IBS subtypes.

steps.dose: 500 mg BID for 4 weeks.
steps.why: Relaxes intestinal smooth muscle and modulates motility via calcium channel blockade, providing relief from abdominal pain and cramping. Particularly effective in IBS with predominant pain or urgency.

steps.dose: 100 billion CFU/day for 8 weeks.
steps.why: Probiotic supplementation supports microbial diversity and improves gut barrier function, reducing bloating, discomfort, and inconsistent stools. Most beneficial when high-dose and multi-strain.

protocols.notes: IBS management requires a multifactorial approach combining dietary precision, targeted supplementation, and stress regulation. Emphasize sleep hygiene, regular physical activity, and avoidance of processed foods, caffeine, and alcohol. Reassess symptoms periodically and adjust interventions based on IBS subtype and individual response.

protocols.title: Small Intestinal Bacterial Overgrowth
protocols.background: Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO) is a condition characterized by excessive or abnormal types of bacteria in the small intestine, leading to impaired digestion and nutrient absorption. Etiologies include impaired intestinal motility (eg, diabetes, scleroderma), structural abnormalities (eg, adhesions, strictures), and reduced gastric acid or pancreatic enzyme secretion. While the exact prevalence is uncertain, SIBO is more common in individuals with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), older adults, and those with prior GI surgery. Pathophysiologically, bacterial overgrowth disrupts nutrient absorption, deconjugates bile salts, and ferments carbohydrates, producing gas and inflammation. Clinical features include bloating, abdominal discomfort, flatulence, diarrhea, and in chronic cases, weight loss or nutrient deficiencies (eg, B12, fat-soluble vitamins). Differential diagnoses include IBS, lactose intolerance, celiac disease, and inflammatory bowel disease. Diagnosis is commonly made using breath tests (glucose or lactulose hydrogen/methane testing) or, less commonly, small bowel aspirate cultures. Management involves treating underlying causes, dietary modification (eg, low FODMAP), and antibiotics such as rifaximin. Prognosis is generally favorable with appropriate treatment, though recurrence is common. Complications may include malnutrition, osteoporosis, or bacterial translocation in severe or untreated cases.

steps.dose: Berberine 500 mg TID + oregano oil (standardized to 55% carvacrol) 200 mg BID x 4 weeks.
steps.why: Broad-spectrum antimicrobial herbs reduce bacterial overgrowth in the small intestine with efficacy comparable to rifaximin. Especially useful for methane-dominant or hydrogen-dominant SIBO, often with fewer systemic side effects than antibiotics.

Exclusive elemental diet providing 1200-1600 kcal/day for 14 days. This specific diet starves bacterial overgrowth by providing pre-digested nutrients that are absorbed early in the small intestine, minimizing substrate for fermentation. Highly effective in breath test normalization.

steps.dose: 2-3 mL tincture of bitters (eg. gentian, artichoke, ginger) 15 minutes before meals.
steps.why: Space meals 4-5 hours apart. Reassess after 6 weeks. Supports activation of the migrating motor complex and bile flow, which clears residual bacteria and prevents stasis. Meal spacing avoids repeated MMC interruption and is crucial for long-term relapse prevention.

steps.dose: Methylcobalamin 1000 mcg/day + vitamin D3 2000 IU/day + magnesium citrate 300 mg/day + iron bisglycinate

steps.agent: 25 mg/day for 8 weeks (or until lab values normalize).
steps.why: Malabsorption in SIBO can cause deficiencies in B12, iron, fat-soluble vitamins, and minerals. Restoring these deficiencies supports energy, gut repair, and immune function during recovery.

protocols.notes: SIBO treatment requires a strategic combination of microbial reduction, motility regulation, and nutrient restoration. Avoid snacking between meals, manage stress, and reassess for underlying contributors like hypochlorhydria or previous antibiotic overuse. Consider follow-up breath testing and gradual diet liberalization after symptoms resolve to support sustainable gut health.

protocols.title: Generalized Anxiety Disorder
protocols.background: Generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) is a chronic psychiatric condition characterized by excessive, uncontrollable worry about various aspects of daily life for at least six months, accompanied by physical symptoms such as restlessness, fatigue, muscle tension, irritability, and sleep disturbances. The etiology is multifactorial, involving genetic predisposition, neurotransmitter imbalances (notably GABA, serotonin, and norepinephrine), and environmental stressors. GAD affects approximately 3-6% of the population, with higher prevalence in women and often co-occurring with depression or other anxiety disorders. Pathophysiologically, GAD is associated with heightened amygdala activity and dysregulation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, leading to persistent hyperarousal and worry. Clinical presentation includes pervasive anxiety not limited to specific triggers, often impairing social or occupational functioning. Differential diagnoses include panic disorder, major depressive disorder, OCD, PTSD, and medical conditions such as hyperthyroidism. Diagnosis is clinical, based on DSM-5 criteria. Management involves cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs), and lifestyle interventions such as exercise and stress reduction. Prognosis is variable; while many improve with treatment, chronic symptoms can lead to reduced quality of life and increased risk for substance use and physical health issues.

steps.dose: 100 mg twice daily for 8 weeks.
steps.why: Promotes alpha brainwave activity and enhances GABA signaling, leading to a calm, focused mental state without sedation. Safe with SSRIs and especially useful for worry, tension, and cognitive hyperarousal in GAD.

steps.dose: 2000 mg EPA daily for 12 weeks.
steps.why: Reduces neuroinflammation and modulates neurotransmitter function associated with mood regulation. Shown in clinical studies to significantly reduce anxiety symptoms in individuals with GAD.

steps.dose: 300 mg daily for 8 weeks.
steps.why: Calms the nervous system by regulating NMDA receptors and supporting parasympathetic tone. Supportive in easing anxiety with muscle tension, restlessness, or sleep disturbance. Especially indicated in patients with poor dietary intake or high stress burden.

steps.dose: 250 mg standardized extract (30% kavalactones) BID for 4 weeks.
steps.why: Acts as a non-sedating anxiolytic by modulating GABA-A receptors and reducing excessive neural excitation. Effective for GAD with prominent worry and tension. Be sure to screen for liver conditions before using.

protocols.notes: GAD responds best to a multimodal plan combining nutritional, botanical, and lifestyle therapies. Encourage regular physical activity, mindfulness-based practices, and consistent, balanced meals. Screen for caffeine overuse and food intolerances. Address underlying stressors and recommend psychotherapy (eg. CBT or ACT) to reinforce long-term resilience.

protocols.title: Major Depressive Disorder
protocols.background: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is a common mood disorder characterized by persistent feelings of sadness, hopelessness, and loss of interest or pleasure in daily activities, lasting at least two weeks and accompanied by symptoms such as changes in sleep, appetite, energy, concentration, and suicidal ideation. Etiology is multifactorial, involving genetic predisposition, neurotransmitter imbalances (eg, serotonin, dopamine, norepinephrine), psychosocial stressors, and medical conditions. MDD affects approximately 7% of adults annually in the U.S., with higher prevalence in women and individuals with a history of trauma or chronic illness. Pathophysiologically, MDD involves dysregulation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, impaired neuroplasticity, and functional changes in brain regions such as the prefrontal cortex and amygdala. Clinically, patients present with emotional, cognitive, and physical symptoms that impair functioning. Differential diagnoses include bipolar disorder, dysthymia, grief, hypothyroidism, and substance-induced mood disorder. Diagnosis is clinical, based on DSM-5 criteria. Management includes psychotherapy (especially cognitive behavioral therapy), pharmacotherapy with antidepressants (eg, SSRIs, SNRIs), and lifestyle interventions; electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) may be used in severe or treatment-resistant cases. Prognosis varies—many respond well to treatment, but recurrence is common. Complications include social withdrawal, impaired occupational functioning, substance abuse, and increased risk of suicide.

steps.dose: 4000 mg EPA daily for 12 weeks.
steps.why: Reduces neuroinflammation and enhances serotonin and dopamine signaling, particularly when combined with SSRIs. Clinical evidence supports its efficacy in cases of moderate to severe depression.

steps.dose: Vitamin D 2000 IU daily for 12 weeks.
steps.why: Supports mood regulation via modulation of inflammatory cytokines and neurotransmitter synthesis. Especially beneficial in individuals with low serum vitamin D or seasonal affective features.

steps.dose: 400 mg twice daily for 8 weeks.
steps.why: Enhances methylation and monoamine synthesis, improving mood and energy. Effective in cases of major depression, but avoid using in bipolar patients due to risk of inducing mania.

Whole-food diet emphasizing vegetables, legumes, fish, olive oil, nuts, and seeds for 12 weeks. Improves depressive symptoms through anti-inflammatory effects, improved nutrient density, and microbiome balance. Supported by the SMILES and HELFIMED trials as a first-line dietary intervention in depression.

protocols.notes: MDD treatment is most effective when combining lifestyle therapy, nutrient support, and counseling. Encourage structured exercise, therapy (CBT, ACT), and social engagement where possible. Screen for iron deficiency, especially in menstruating individuals. Consider incorporating adjunct botanicals such as St. John’s wort or rhodiola based on subtype and medication use.

protocols.title: Eczema
protocols.background: Eczema, or atopic dermatitis, is a chronic, relapsing inflammatory skin condition characterized by dry, itchy, and inflamed skin. It typically begins in childhood and is associated with a personal or family history of atopy, including asthma and allergic rhinitis. Etiology is multifactorial, involving genetic mutations (notably filaggrin), immune dysregulation, and environmental triggers such as allergens, irritants, and climate. Eczema affects up to 20% of children and 10% of adults worldwide. Pathophysiologically, a defective skin barrier allows increased transepidermal water loss and allergen penetration, triggering Th2-mediated inflammation and cytokine release. Clinically, eczema presents with pruritic, erythematous patches, often with lichenification or excoriation, typically on the face and extensor surfaces in children and flexural areas in adults. Differential diagnoses include contact dermatitis, psoriasis, seborrheic dermatitis, and scabies. Diagnosis is clinical based on history and exam findings. Management includes emollients, topical corticosteroids or calcineurin inhibitors, antihistamines, and avoidance of triggers. Severe cases may require systemic immunomodulators or biologics (eg, dupilumab). Prognosis varies - many children improve with age, though relapses are common. Complications include secondary infections, sleep disturbance, and reduced quality of life.

steps.why: Eliminate eggs, dairy, and wheat for 4 weeks, guided by IgE serology. These aforementioned common food intolerances can trigger or worsen eczema through immune activation and increased gut permeability. This approach targets underlying inflammation while helping identify dietary triggers specific to the patient. Consider food reintroduction after symptom stabilization.

steps.dose: 2000 mg daily GLA-containing oil (evening primrose or hempseed oil) for 8 weeks.
steps.why: γ-Linolenic acid bypasses dysfunctional delta-6-desaturase activity, reducing pro-inflammatory leukotriene formation and improving skin hydration, itch, and lesion severity. Clinically effective in many cases despite mixed evidence in trials.
