steps.why: Modulates inflammatory pathways and enhances skin barrier integrity by shifting the omega-6:3 ratio May reduce lesion severity and is especially helpful in those with coexisting atopic conditions.

steps.why: Vitamin D supports immune regulation and skin barrier function, with supplementation shown to reduce eczema severity, especially during the winter or in patients with low baseline levels.

protocols.notes: Eczema is a multifactorial condition involving immune dysregulation, skin barrier dysfunction, and environmental triggers. Combining dietary elimination, targeted fatty acid support, and nutrient repletion offers strong foundational care. Consider topical herbal applications (eg. calendula, aloe), hydrotherapy, and probiotics as adjuncts. Reassess nutritional status and reintroduce foods cautiously to monitor tolerance over time.

protocols.title: Psoriasis
protocols.background: Psoriasis is a chronic, immune-mediated skin disorder characterized by hyperproliferation of keratinocytes and systemic inflammation, most commonly presenting as well-demarcated, scaly erythematous plaques. The etiology involves a combination of genetic predisposition and environmental triggers such as infections, trauma, stress, and certain medications. Psoriasis affects about 2-3% of the global population and can occur at any age, with peaks in young adulthood and mid-life. Pathophysiologically, psoriasis involves dysregulated T-cell activity - particularly Th1 and Th17 pathways - leading to cytokine release (eg, TNF-α, IL-17, IL-23) and accelerated skin cell turnover. Clinical presentation includes thick, silver-scaled plaques on extensor surfaces, scalp, and lower back, often with pruritus or burning; nail pitting and psoriatic arthritis may also occur. Differential diagnoses include eczema, tinea corporis, seborrheic dermatitis, and cutaneous lupus. Diagnosis is clinical but may be confirmed by skin biopsy. Management depends on severity and includes topical agents (corticosteroids, vitamin D analogs), phototherapy, and systemic therapies (methotrexate, biologics targeting TNF-α or IL-23). Prognosis is chronic but manageable; complications may include joint damage from psoriatic arthritis, metabolic syndrome, and psychosocial distress.

steps.why: Adopt a Mediterranean-style whole foods diet incorporating ≥5 servings/day of vegetables/fruits, olive oil as primary fat

steps.why: This dietary pattern reduces systemic inflammation and psoriasis severity by lowering oxidative stress and improving metabolic and immune function. Strong evidence supports improvement in PASI scores with dietary adherence and modest weight loss.

steps.dose: 4000 mg daily of combined EPA/DHA for 12 weeks.
steps.why: Functions to decrease pro-inflammatory eicosanoid production and shifts the omega-3:6 balance in favor of anti- inflammatory activity. Supports resolution of plaque and joint symptoms, with added cardiovascular benefit in psoriatic arthritis.

steps.dose: 2000 IU/day for 12 weeks.
steps.why: Titrate as necessary to achieve serum 25(OH)D of ~45 ng/mL. Vitamin D regulates keratinocyte turnover and modulates immune function in psoriatic skin. Supplementation is effective for reducing lesion severity, especially in those with documented deficiency or limited sun exposure.

steps.dose: Apply aloe vera gel or calendula cream twice daily to affected areas for 4 weeks.
steps.why: Soothes inflamed skin, reduces itching and scaling, and promotes epithelial healing. Clinically useful as an adjunct to dietary therapy or conventional topicals, especially in mild to moderate cases of plaque psoriasis.

protocols.notes: Psoriasis management benefits from addressing systemic inflammation, nutrient status, and skin-level irritation. Combine dietary therapy, omega-3 supplementation, and vitamin D with gentle, anti-inflammatory topicals for a comprehensive approach. Consider testing for gliadin antibodies, minimizing alcohol, and supporting mental well-being to improve outcomes.

protocols.title: Acne Vulgaris
protocols.background: Acne vulgaris is a common chronic inflammatory skin disorder affecting the pilosebaceous unit, primarily seen during adolescence but also present in adults. It is caused by a combination of excess sebum production, follicular hyperkeratinization, Cutibacterium acnes colonization, and inflammation. Contributing factors include hormonal changes (especially androgens), genetics, stress, and certain medications or cosmetics. Acne affects up to 85% of teenagers and may persist into adulthood, particularly in women. Pathophysiologically, blocked hair follicles become comedones, which may develop into inflammatory papules, pustules, nodules, or cysts. It typically presents on the face, chest, and back. Differential diagnoses include rosacea, folliculitis, perioral dermatitis, and keratosis pilaris. Diagnosis is clinical based on lesion morphology and distribution. Management depends on severity and may include topical agents (benzoyl peroxide, retinoids, antibiotics), oral antibiotics, hormonal therapy (eg, oral contraceptives), and isotretinoin for severe cases. Prognosis is favorable with treatment, though relapses are common. Complications include scarring, post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, and psychosocial impact such as anxiety or low self-esteem.

This plan addresses systemic drivers while supporting skin healing and barrier integrity. Consider adjunctive therapies like probiotics, liver-supportive herbs (eg. burdock, dandelion), and stress modulation to approach this comprehensively. Reassess every 6-8 weeks for clinical progress and adjust doses as needed.

protocols.title: Warts
protocols.background: Warts are benign epidermal growths caused by human papillomavirus (HPV) infection, most commonly types 1, 2, 4, 6, and 11. Transmission occurs through direct skin-to-skin contact or contaminated surfaces, often facilitated by breaks in the skin. Warts are common worldwide, particularly in immunocompromised individuals and children, with varying presentations depending on the HPV type and location. Pathophysiologically, HPV infects basal keratinocytes, promoting uncontrolled cell proliferation and forming verrucous lesions. Clinical types include common warts (verruca vulgaris), plantar warts, flat warts, and anogenital warts. Differential diagnoses include seborrheic keratosis, calluses, molluscum contagiosum, and squamous cell carcinoma. Diagnosis is clinical based on lesion appearance; biopsy is rarely needed. Management includes cryotherapy, salicylic acid, laser therapy, or immunomodulatory treatments. Prognosis is generally good, as many warts resolve spontaneously, though recurrence is common. Complications may include pain (especially plantar warts), cosmetic concerns, and, rarely, malignant transformation in immunosuppressed patients or with high-risk HPV types.

steps.dose: Apply sliced fresh garlic clove directly on the wart. Cover with bandage. Replace daily for 2 weeks.
steps.why: Garlic has potent antiviral, immune-stimulating, and keratolytic effects, contributing to wart regression.
Apply a thin layer (~0.5 cm length strip per wart) of 15% sinecatechins ointment (eg. Veregen) directly to the wart three

steps.why: Sinecatechins are standardized green tea polyphenols shown to have antiviral and antioxidant effects, likely helpful in immune modulation against HPV .

Apply standard duct tape over the wart continuously, replacing the tape every 5 days for up to 6 weeks. The occlusive environment may stimulate local immune response and physically irritate the lesion, helping eliminate the wart. This low-cost method has modest supportive evidence.

steps.why: Traditionally used for viral skin lesions and is thought to have immunomodulatory and antiviral actions.

protocols.notes: Warts are caused by low-risk strains of HPV and often resolve spontaneously, but persistent cases benefit from combined approaches. Topical therapies aim to disrupt the lesion and stimulate local immune activity. For recurrent cases, consider dietary garlic, zinc supplementation, and evaluation of immune status. Educate patients on consistent application and the importance of skin monitoring for irritation.

protocols.title: Burns
protocols.background: Burns are injuries to the skin and underlying tissues caused by heat, chemicals, electricity, radiation, or friction. Sunburns are a common type of superficial burn resulting from excessive ultraviolet (UV) radiation exposure. Burns are categorized by depth - first-degree (superficial), second-degree (partial-thickness), and third-degree (full-thickness) - and severity is assessed based on total body surface area (TBSA) affected. Etiologies include household accidents, fire exposure, industrial incidents, and prolonged sun exposure. Globally, burns are a significant cause of morbidity, particularly in children and low-income settings. Pathophysiologically, burns cause direct tissue injury, capillary leakage, inflammation, and in severe cases, systemic responses like hypovolemia or shock. Clinical presentation depends on severity and may include erythema, blistering, pain, edema, or eschar formation. Sunburn typically presents with redness, tenderness, and peeling. Differential diagnoses include contact dermatitis, cellulitis, and photosensitive eruptions. Diagnosis is clinical, based on history and burn characteristics. Management ranges from supportive care (cool compresses, hydration, analgesics, topical antimicrobials) to advanced wound care and fluid resuscitation for extensive burns. Prognosis depends on burn depth, size, and comorbidities; mild burns heal well, but severe burns may lead to infection, scarring, contractures, or systemic complications such as sepsis or organ failure.

steps.why: Manuka honey provides broad-spectrum antimicrobial protection and maintains a moist wound environment that promotes tissue regeneration. It also helps debride necrotic tissue and reduce inflammation, making it ideal for superficial to partial-thickness burns.

Apply a generous layer of pure, inner leaf aloe vera gel to the affected area 2-3 times daily. Aloe functions to soothe pain, reduce local inflammation, and support epithelial cell migration. Aloe is particularly effective during the initial healing phase and may help prevent scarring if used consistently.
Once the wound is clean and free of active exudate, apply a thin layer of 0.2% hyaluronic acid gel topically twice daily

Hyaluronic acid helps retain moisture at the wound site, reduces discomfort, and supports collagen synthesis and tissue remodeling. It is best used in the re-epithelialization stage when tissue is regenerating.

steps.why: Vitamin C enhances collagen synthesis and immune defense, while zinc plays a critical role in wound healing and inflammation regulation.

protocols.notes: This plan is appropriate for minor outpatient burns and supports both infection control and tissue repair naturally; however, for severe burns or those covering large body areas, refer to emergency care.

protocols.title: Scars
protocols.background: Scars are the fibrous tissue that replaces normal skin following injury, representing the end stage of wound healing. Etiologies include surgical incisions, trauma, burns, infections, or inflammatory skin conditions like acne. Nearly everyone develops scars at some point, but the severity and appearance vary based on genetic factors, wound depth, location, and healing response. Pathophysiologically, scars form as fibroblasts deposit collagen during the proliferative and remodeling phases of healing. While most scars are flat and pale, abnormal healing may lead to hypertrophic scars (raised but within the wound margins) or keloids (overgrowth beyond the original wound). Clinical presentation depends on type, size, and location. Differential diagnoses include dermatofibroma, epidermal inclusion cysts, or neoplastic lesions. Diagnosis is clinical. Management may include topical therapies (silicone gel, corticosteroids), laser treatment, pressure therapy, or surgical revision in severe cases. Prognosis is generally good for functional recovery, though cosmetic or psychosocial impact may persist. Complications include restricted movement (especially over joints), chronic pain, or recurrence of keloids.

steps.why: Vitamin E has antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects supporting tissue remodeling.

steps.why: Centella promotes fibroblast activity and collagen remodeling, reducing hypertrophic scar formation.

protocols.notes: Scarring is a normal part of wound healing, but early intervention may reduce hypertrophic or keloid formation. Encourage gentle scar massage and correct vitamin D deficiency in at-risk individuals.
